glossary.readjustment of seats after census: The Article 82 requirement that, after each census, Lok Sabha seat allocation among States and constituency boundaries within States be readjusted by an authority and method Parliament fixes by law.
glossary.Delimitation Commission (readjustment au: The body Parliament has historically established by law to carry out the Article 82 readjustment of parliamentary seat allocation and constituency boundaries after each census.
glossary.readjustment not affecting current House: The first proviso to Article 82, ensuring that any constituency readjustment does not alter the composition or representation of the currently sitting House of the People — it applies only from the next dissolution onward.
glossary.delimitation freeze until post-2026 cens: The third proviso to Article 82, which — paralleling Article 81(3) — suspends the obligation to readjust Lok Sabha seat allocation and constituency boundaries until the first census after 2026 is published.
glossary.Council of States is a permanent body: The Article 83(1) rule that the Rajya Sabha is never dissolved as a body, distinguishing it structurally from the Lok Sabha, which has a fixed term and is dissolved either on term expiry or earlier.
glossary.one-third retirement every two years (Ra: The Article 83(1) mechanism by which approximately one-third of Rajya Sabha members retire every second year on a staggered basis, per rules Parliament makes by law, preserving the House's institutional continuity.
glossary.five-year term of the House of the Peopl: The Article 83(2) rule fixing the Lok Sabha's term at five years from the date of its first meeting, after which it automatically dissolves unless dissolved earlier — a figure that was briefly extended to six years by the 42nd Amendment (1976) and restored to five by the 44th Amendment (1978).
glossary.Emergency extension of Lok Sabha term: The proviso to Article 83(2) allowing Parliament to extend the Lok Sabha's five-year term by law during an operating Proclamation of Emergency, in increments of up to one year at a time, capped at six months after the Emergency ends.
glossary.citizenship and pre-election oath (Parli: The Article 84(a) qualification requiring a prospective Member of Parliament to be an Indian citizen and to make and subscribe the prescribed Third Schedule oath or affirmation before an Election Commission-authorised person before candidacy.
glossary.thirty years minimum age (Rajya Sabha): The Article 84(b) minimum age of thirty years required for a person to be chosen to a Council of States (Rajya Sabha) seat.
glossary.twenty-five years minimum age (Lok Sabha: The Article 84(b) minimum age of twenty-five years required for a person to be chosen to a House of the People (Lok Sabha) seat.
glossary.other qualifications prescribed by Parli: The Article 84(c) residual power allowing Parliament to prescribe, by ordinary law (chiefly the Representation of the People Act, 1951), further qualifications for Parliamentary membership beyond citizenship, oath, and age.
glossary.summoning of Parliament: The Article 85(1) Presidential power to summon each House of Parliament to meet at a time and place of the President's choosing, subject to the mandatory maximum six-month gap between sessions.
glossary.six-month gap rule between sessions: The Article 85(1) requirement that no more than six months elapse between the last sitting of one Parliamentary session and the first sitting of the next, guaranteeing Parliament meets at least twice a year.
glossary.prorogation of Houses: The Article 85(2)(a) Presidential power to formally end a Parliamentary session (prorogue) without dissolving the House, distinct from dissolution which ends the House's very existence.
glossary.dissolution of the House of the People (: The Article 85(2)(b) Presidential power to dissolve the Lok Sabha specifically — a power that cannot be exercised against the permanent Council of States under Article 83(1).
glossary.President's right to address Parliament: The Article 86(1) discretionary power of the President to address either House or both Houses assembled together on any occasion, with power to require members' attendance.
glossary.President's power to send messages to Ho: The Article 86(2) power of the President to send messages to either House on any matter, Bill-related or otherwise, obliging that House to consider the message's subject with all convenient despatch.
glossary.President's Special Address: The mandatory address under Article 87(1) that the President must deliver to both Houses assembled together at the start of the first session after each general election and the first session of each year, informing Parliament of the causes of its summons.
glossary.commencement of first session after gene: One of the two mandatory triggers under Article 87(1) for the President's Special Address — the opening of Parliament's first session following a fresh general election to the House of the People.
glossary.commencement of first session of each ye: The second mandatory trigger under Article 87(1) for the President's Special Address — the opening of Parliament's first session of every calendar year.
glossary.Ministers' right to speak in either Hous: The Article 88 right of every Minister to speak in and otherwise participate in the proceedings of either House, any joint sitting, and any committee they are named to, regardless of which House (if any) they are a member of.
glossary.Attorney-General's right to speak in Par: The Article 88 right of the Attorney-General for India, though not an elected member of either House, to speak in and participate in the proceedings of either House, joint sittings, and named committees.
glossary.no voting right by virtue of Article 88: The express limitation in Article 88 that the right to speak and participate it grants does not itself confer any voting right — a Minister or the Attorney-General votes only if independently a member of the relevant House.
glossary.Deputy Chairman of the Council of States: The presiding officer the Rajya Sabha elects from among its own members under Article 89(2), distinct from the ex officio Chairman (the Vice-President), governed as to tenure and removal by Article 90.
glossary.automatic vacation of Deputy Chairman of: The Article 90(a) rule that a Deputy Chairman of the Council of States automatically vacates that office on ceasing to be a member of the Council for any reason.
glossary.Deputy Chairman resignation to Chairman: The Article 90(b) mechanism by which a Deputy Chairman of the Council of States may resign by writing under his hand addressed to the Chairman.
glossary.removal of Deputy Chairman by Council re: The Article 90(c) removal mechanism — a simple-majority resolution of all then members of the Council of States, moved only after at least fourteen days' advance notice.
glossary.Deputy Chairman performing Chairman's du: The Article 91(1) rule that the Deputy Chairman performs the Chairman's duties whenever the Chairmanship is vacant, or whenever the Vice-President is acting as or discharging the functions of President under Article 65, with a further fallback to a President-appointed Council member if the Deputy Chairmanship is also vacant.
glossary.acting Chairman during a sitting: The Article 91(2) fallback for mere absence (not vacancy) of the Chairman from a specific Rajya Sabha sitting — the Deputy Chairman acts, or failing that a person determined under the Council's rules of procedure, or failing that a person the Council itself determines.
glossary.no presiding over own removal resolution: The Article 92(1) natural-justice rule barring the Chairman from presiding while a resolution for the Vice-President's removal is under consideration, and barring the Deputy Chairman from presiding while a resolution for his own removal is under consideration.
glossary.Chairman's speaking right without voting: The Article 92(2) rule permitting the Chairman to speak and participate in debate on a resolution for the Vice-President's removal, while completely denying him any vote at all — on that resolution or any other matter — during those proceedings, overriding the general voting rule in Article 100.
glossary.Speaker of the House of the People: The Lok Sabha's chief presiding officer, elected from among its own members under Article 93, whose tenure and removal are governed by Article 94, including a special continuity rule during dissolution.
glossary.Deputy Speaker of the House of the Peopl: The Lok Sabha's secondary presiding officer, elected from among its own members under Article 93 alongside the Speaker, whose tenure and removal are governed by Article 94.
glossary.automatic vacation of Speaker/Deputy Spe: The Article 94(a) rule that a Speaker or Deputy Speaker of the House of the People automatically vacates that office on ceasing to be a House member, subject to the Speaker's special dissolution-continuity proviso.
glossary.resignation of Speaker to Deputy Speaker: The Article 94(b) mechanism by which the Speaker resigns by writing addressed to the Deputy Speaker, and the Deputy Speaker resigns by writing addressed to the Speaker.
glossary.removal of Speaker by House resolution: The Article 94(c) removal mechanism — a simple-majority resolution of all then members of the House of the People, moved only after at least fourteen days' advance notice.
glossary.Speaker's continuity despite dissolution: The second proviso to Article 94 uniquely protecting the Speaker (not the Deputy Speaker) from automatically vacating office on dissolution of the House of the People — the Speaker continues until immediately before the newly constituted House's first meeting.
glossary.Deputy Speaker performing Speaker's duti: The Article 95(1) rule that the Deputy Speaker performs the Speaker's duties whenever the Speakership is vacant, with a further fallback to a President-appointed House member if the Deputy Speakership is also vacant.
glossary.acting Speaker during a sitting: The Article 95(2) fallback for mere absence (not vacancy) of the Speaker from a specific Lok Sabha sitting — the Deputy Speaker acts, or failing that a person determined under the House's rules of procedure, or failing that a person the House itself determines.
glossary.no presiding over own removal resolution: The Article 96(1) natural-justice rule barring the Speaker from presiding while a resolution for his own removal is under consideration, and barring the Deputy Speaker from presiding while a resolution for his own removal is under consideration.
glossary.Speaker's limited voting right during ow: The Article 96(2) rule permitting the Speaker to speak, participate, and vote in the first instance during debate on his own removal resolution, while denying only the tie-breaking casting vote he would otherwise exercise under Article 100 — a narrower restriction than the Rajya Sabha Chairman's total voting ban under Article 92(2).
glossary.salaries of presiding officers (Article: The Article 97 rule fixing salaries and allowances for the Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Council of States and the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of the People, as Parliament determines by law or, absent such law, as specified in the Second Schedule.
glossary.separate secretarial staff for each Hous: The Article 98(1) default rule that each House of Parliament has its own separate secretariat, protecting Parliament's administrative independence from the executive.
glossary.common posts between the two Houses: The proviso to Article 98(1) permitting the creation of staff posts common to both Houses of Parliament, despite the general rule that each House has a separate secretariat.
glossary.Parliament's law-making power over secre: The Article 98(2) power of Parliament to regulate by law the recruitment and conditions of service of persons appointed to either House's secretarial staff.
glossary.President's interim rule-making power fo: The Article 98(3) power allowing the President, after consulting the Speaker or the Chairman as relevant, to make interim rules on secretariat recruitment and service conditions until Parliament legislates under clause (2), with such rules always subject to any later Parliamentary law.
glossary.oath of office (Member of Parliament): The Article 99 requirement that every Member of Parliament, before taking his seat, make and subscribe an oath or affirmation before the President (or a person appointed by the President) in the form set out in the Third Schedule — distinct from the Article 84(a) oath taken before candidacy, and backed by the Article 104 penalty for non-compliance.
glossary.majority of members present and voting: The Article 100(1) default rule that, except as otherwise constitutionally provided, all questions in either House of Parliament are decided by a majority of the members present and voting, excluding the presiding officer.
glossary.presiding officer's casting vote: The Article 100(1) rule that the person presiding over a House of Parliament does not vote in the first instance but exercises a casting vote in the case of an equality of votes — contrasted with the narrower version of this rule discussed under Article 96(2).
glossary.validity despite vacancies: The Article 100(3) rule that the proceedings of Parliament remain valid notwithstanding that it is later discovered some person who was not entitled to do so sat, voted, or otherwise participated in a House's proceedings.
glossary.validity despite ineligible participatio: The Article 100(3) safeguard preserving the validity of Parliamentary proceedings even where an unqualified or disqualified person sat or voted, protecting legislative business from retrospective invalidation.
glossary.quorum for Parliament (one-tenth rule): The Article 100(3) default quorum — one-tenth of the total membership of the House — required to constitute a meeting of either House of Parliament, subject to Parliament's power to prescribe otherwise by law, coupled with the presiding officer's Article 100(4) duty to adjourn or suspend the sitting when quorum is lacking.
glossary.no simultaneous membership of both House: The Article 101(1) bar on a person being a member of both the Council of States and the House of the People at the same time, with Parliament empowered to make laws on vacating one seat if elected to both.
glossary.no simultaneous membership of Parliament: The Article 101(2) bar on a person being a member both of Parliament and of a State Legislature simultaneously, subject to a grace period Parliament prescribes by law for vacating one seat, after which the Parliament seat becomes vacant automatically.
glossary.seat vacation on disqualification (Artic: The Article 101(3)(a) rule that a sitting member's seat automatically becomes vacant upon incurring any of the disqualifications specified in Article 102.
glossary.resignation of parliamentary seat: The Article 101(3)(b) mechanism by which a member resigns his seat by writing addressed to the Chairman or the Speaker as applicable, with the seat becoming vacant upon acceptance, subject to the presiding officer's inquiry into the resignation's genuineness.
glossary.presiding officer's inquiry into genuine: The proviso to Article 101(3)(b), added by the 33rd Amendment (1974), empowering the Chairman or Speaker to withhold acceptance of a resignation if satisfied, after such inquiry as he thinks fit, that it is not voluntary or genuine — a safeguard against coerced or fraudulent resignations.
glossary.sixty-day absence seat vacation: The Article 101(4) rule that a House may declare a member's seat vacant if he is absent from all its sittings for sixty days without the House's permission, excluding periods of prorogation or adjournment for more than four consecutive days from that computation.
glossary.office of profit disqualification (Parli: The Article 102(1)(a) disqualification of a person holding any office of profit under the Government of India or a State (other than an office Parliament by law declares does not disqualify), subject to the Explanation exempting Ministers from being deemed to hold an office of profit by reason only of their ministerial office.
glossary.unsound mind disqualification: The Article 102(1)(b) disqualification of a person of unsound mind, so declared by a competent court, from being chosen as or remaining a Member of Parliament.
glossary.undischarged insolvent disqualification: The Article 102(1)(c) disqualification of an undischarged insolvent from being chosen as or remaining a Member of Parliament.
glossary.foreign citizenship or allegiance disqua: The Article 102(1)(d) disqualification of a person who is not an Indian citizen, or who has voluntarily acquired foreign citizenship, or who acknowledges allegiance or adherence to a foreign State.
glossary.Parliament-prescribed disqualification (: The residual Article 102(1)(e) disqualification ground allowing Parliament to prescribe further disqualifications by law, chiefly exercised through the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
glossary.Tenth Schedule disqualification (anti-de: The Article 102(2) disqualification for defection under the Tenth Schedule, inserted by the 52nd Amendment (1985), which operates as a separate self-contained disqualification regime with its own Speaker/Chairman-centred adjudication procedure distinct from Article 103's Election Commission-based procedure for Article 102(1) grounds.
glossary.President's decision on Article 102(1) d: The Article 103(1) rule that questions on whether a sitting member has become subject to any Article 102(1) disqualification are decided by the President, whose decision is final.
glossary.mandatory Election Commission opinion (A: The Article 103(2) requirement that before deciding any Article 102(1) disqualification question, the President must obtain and act according to the Election Commission's opinion — making the Commission the real decision-maker in substance despite the formal vesting of the decision in the President.
glossary.penalty for sitting/voting without oath: The Article 104 penalty of five hundred rupees for each day a person sits or votes as a Member of Parliament knowing he has not complied with the Article 99 oath requirement, or knowing he is not qualified or is disqualified for membership — recoverable as a debt due to the Union.
glossary.freedom of speech in Parliament: The Article 105(1) guarantee of freedom of speech in Parliament, subject to the Constitution's other provisions and to the rules and standing orders regulating Parliamentary procedure.
glossary.immunity from court proceedings for parl: The Article 105(2) absolute immunity barring any court from instituting proceedings against a Member of Parliament in respect of anything said or any vote given by him in Parliament or any Parliamentary committee.
glossary.immunity for authorised publication of p: The Article 105(2) protection extending court-proceeding immunity to any person for publishing, under the authority of either House, any report, paper, votes, or proceedings of that House.
glossary.residual powers privileges and immunitie: The Article 105(3) provision defining the powers, privileges, and immunities of each House of Parliament and its members and committees as those Parliament defines by law from time to time, and until so defined, those of the House of Commons of the UK Parliament as they stood immediately before the commencement of the Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment position) — the 44th Amendment (1979) having removed an earlier evolving-UK-precedent link in favour of this fixed pre-commencement baseline.
glossary.extension of privileges to non-member pa: The Article 105(4) provision extending the Article 105 privileges and immunities to persons who, though not members, are entitled under the Constitution (such as the Attorney-General or Ministers under Article 88) to speak in and otherwise take part in the proceedings of a House or its committees.
glossary.salaries and allowances of Members of Pa: The Article 106 rule that Members of both Houses receive salaries and allowances as Parliament determines by law, defaulting — absent such law — to the rates payable to Constituent Assembly of the Dominion of India members immediately before the Constitution's commencement, rather than to any Second Schedule figure (unlike the salary defaults for the President, Ministers, and presiding officers under Articles 59, 75, and 97).
glossary.dual-origin of Bills: The Article 107(1) default rule that an ordinary Bill may originate in either House of Parliament, subject to the Money Bill and financial Bill restrictions in Articles 109 and 117 which confine those categories to the House of the People.
glossary.prorogation does not lapse a Bill: The Article 107(3) rule that a Bill pending in Parliament survives the prorogation (formal ending) of a session and carries over to the next session, contrasted with dissolution which is generally fatal to a pending Bill under Article 107(4)-(5).
glossary.dissolution lapses Lok Sabha-pending Bil: The Article 107(5) rule that a Bill still pending in the House of the People, or passed by it but still pending in the Council of States, lapses upon dissolution of the House of the People — subject to the Article 108(5) exception where a joint sitting has already been notified.
glossary.deadlock between the two Houses: The Article 108(1) trigger conditions for a joint sitting of Parliament — outright rejection of a Bill by the second House, irreconcilable disagreement over amendments, or six months' inaction by the second House after receiving the Bill.
glossary.President's notification of joint sittin: The Article 108(1) discretionary power of the President, once a deadlock trigger arises, to notify both Houses of his intention to summon them to a joint sitting to deliberate and vote on a Bill — unavailable for Money Bills.
glossary.joint sitting majority (both Houses comb: The Article 108(4) voting rule at a joint sitting — the Bill passes if agreed to by a majority of the total membership of both Houses present and voting together, a mechanism that numerically favours the larger House of the People.
glossary.amendments admissible at a joint sitting: The restrictive proviso to Article 108(4) limiting amendments at a joint sitting to those made necessary by delay or those addressing points of continuing disagreement between the Houses, with the presiding officer's ruling on admissibility being final.
glossary.joint sitting survives intervening disso: The Article 108(5) exception to the general dissolution-lapsing rule — once the President has notified an intention to summon a joint sitting, a subsequent dissolution of the House of the People does not prevent the joint sitting from being held and the Bill passed.
glossary.Money Bill introduction restricted to Lo: The Article 109(1) rule that a Money Bill can only be introduced in the House of the People, never in the Council of States.
glossary.fourteen-day recommendation window (Rajy: The Article 109(2) strict time limit within which the Council of States must return a Money Bill to the House of the People with its recommendations, after which the Bill is deemed passed in its original form under Article 109(5).
glossary.Lok Sabha's power to accept or reject Ra: The Article 109(2)-(4) rule giving the House of the People unfettered, unreviewable discretion to accept or reject, wholly or partly, any recommendation the Council of States makes on a Money Bill.
glossary.deemed passage on expiry of fourteen day: The Article 109(5) fallback rule that a Money Bill not returned by the Council of States within fourteen days is automatically deemed passed by both Houses in the form the House of the People originally passed it.
glossary.Money Bill definitional test (Article 11: The exhaustive, closed-list test in Article 110(1) under which a Bill qualifies as a Money Bill only if it deals exclusively with the seven listed fiscal matters — taxation, government borrowing, the Consolidated/Contingency Funds, appropriation, charged expenditure, and Union/State audit-related receipts — or matters merely incidental to them.
glossary.'contains only provisions' requirement: The restrictive word 'only' in Article 110(1), which makes the Money Bill definition exhaustive — a Bill mixing a genuine fiscal matter with any substantive non-fiscal provision fails the Money Bill test even if fiscal matters predominate.
glossary.carve-outs from Money Bill status (Artic: The Article 110(2) exclusions clarifying that a Bill is not a Money Bill merely because it imposes fines, pecuniary penalties, licence or service fees, or because it deals with local-authority taxation for local purposes.
glossary.Speaker's certification of a Money Bill: The Article 110(4) mandatory endorsement — the Speaker of the House of the People's signed certificate that a Bill is a Money Bill — required when the Bill is transmitted to the Council of States under Article 109 and when presented to the President for assent under Article 111.
glossary.finality of Speaker's Money Bill classif: The Article 110(3) rule declaring the Speaker's decision on whether a Bill is a Money Bill to be final — textually conclusive, though its practical finality has been contested in modern litigation over Bills bundling fiscal and non-fiscal provisions (e.g., the Aadhaar Act, 2016 and later Finance Acts).
glossary.Presidential assent to Bills: The Article 111 act by which the President formally approves a Bill passed by both Houses of Parliament, upon which it becomes an Act of Parliament.
glossary.Presidential withholding of assent: The Article 111 option available to the President to decline assent to a Bill outright, an option that — unlike the return-for-reconsideration proviso — carries no textual obligation to explain or to act within any timeframe, and has never been formally exercised against a Bill re-passed after reconsideration.
glossary.President's power to return a Bill for r: The proviso to Article 111 permitting the President, for any Bill except a Money Bill, to return it once to the Houses with a message suggesting reconsideration or specific amendments, without indefinitely blocking it since re-passage compels assent.
glossary.mandatory assent on Bill's re-passage: The concluding rule of the Article 111 proviso — once Parliament re-passes a returned Bill, with or without the President's suggested amendments, the President is constitutionally barred from withholding assent any further.
glossary.annual financial statement (the Union Bu: The Article 112(1) formal name for what is popularly called the Union Budget — the President's mandatory annual statement to both Houses of Parliament of the Government of India's estimated receipts and expenditure for the coming financial year.
glossary.expenditure charged on the Consolidated: The Article 112(3) closed list of expenditure items — including the President's and presiding officers' emoluments, public debt servicing, higher judiciary and CAG salaries/pensions, and court/arbitral award payments — that are insulated from an up-or-down Parliamentary vote under Article 113(1), though open to discussion.
glossary.revenue account vs. other expenditure: The Article 112(2) requirement that the annual financial statement distinguish expenditure on revenue account (recurring/operational spending) from other (typically capital) expenditure, in addition to the separate charged-versus-voted distinction.
glossary.exemption of charged expenditure from vo: The Article 113(1) rule that expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India is not put to a Parliamentary vote — it may be discussed in either House but cannot be approved, rejected, or altered by vote.
glossary.demands for grants: The Article 113(2) mechanism by which non-charged ('voted') expenditure estimates are placed before the House of the People department-by-department for its assent, refusal, or reduction — the constitutional basis of the Indian Budget session's grant-voting and 'cut motion' practice.
glossary.House of the People's power to reduce or: The Article 113(2) rule that the Lok Sabha may assent to a demand for grant in full, refuse it, or reduce the amount specified — but has no power to increase any demand beyond what is proposed.
glossary.Presidential recommendation precondition: The Article 113(3) requirement that no demand for a grant may be made in the House of the People except on the President's prior recommendation, reinforcing exclusive executive initiation of spending proposals.
glossary.Appropriation Bill: The Bill required by Article 114(1), introduced after grants are voted under Article 113, that formally authorises withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund of India of the moneys needed to cover both the voted grants and the fixed charged expenditure.
glossary.bar on amendments varying grants or char: The Article 114(2) rule barring any amendment to an Appropriation Bill in either House that would alter the amount or destination of a voted grant, or vary the amount of charged expenditure, with the presiding officer's ruling on inadmissibility being final.
glossary.no withdrawal from Consolidated Fund wit: The Article 114(3) bedrock rule that no money may be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India except under an appropriation made by law passed under this article, subject only to the interim/exceptional mechanisms of Articles 115 and 116.

sections.title: Name and territory of the Union
sections.raw_text: (1) India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States. (2) The States and the territories thereof shall be as specified in the First Schedule. (3) The territory of India shall comprise— (a) the territories of the States; (b) the Union territories specified in the First Schedule; and (c) such other territories as may be acquired.

breakdown.plain_summary: This opening Article fixes the country's two names — India and Bharat — and declares its basic constitutional character: it is a 'Union' of States, not a loose federation that States could choose to leave. Clause (2) points to the First Schedule for the actual list of States and their territorial extent, and clause (3) explains that India's territory is made up of three things: the States themselves, Union territories (areas administered more directly by the Centre, like Delhi or Chandigarh), and any other territory India may acquire in future (by cession, purchase, or other lawful means).
essential_elements: India is declared a 'Union of States', not a federation of independent units with a right to secede
The specific States and their territories are listed in the First Schedule, not spelled out in Article 1 itself
Indian territory comprises State territories, Union territory areas, and any territory acquired afterward
exceptions_and_qualifications: The word 'Union' was deliberately chosen over 'Federation' to signal that no State has a constitutional right to secede from India
Acquisition of new territory under clause (3)(c) does not by itself require a constitutional amendment — see Article 4
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat Article 1 as the Constitution's opening declaration of statehood and territorial identity — read it together with the First Schedule (which lists the States and Union territories by name) and Article 3 (which lets Parliament reorganise those very territories by ordinary law).

sections.title: Admission or establishment of new States
sections.raw_text: Parliament may by law admit into the Union, or establish, new States on such terms and conditions as it thinks fit.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 2 gives Parliament the power to bring entirely new States into India — either by 'admitting' a State that already exists elsewhere (for example, a former princely state or foreign territory that has acceded to India) or by 'establishing' a wholly new State from scratch. Parliament can attach whatever terms and conditions it thinks fit to that admission or establishment, by ordinary legislation.
essential_elements: Power vests exclusively in Parliament, exercised by ordinary law (not necessarily a constitutional amendment)
Covers two distinct situations: admitting an existing external territory, or establishing a new State
Parliament has wide discretion to fix terms and conditions of admission/establishment
exceptions_and_qualifications: Article 2 deals with bringing in territory from outside India's existing boundaries; Article 3 deals with reorganising territory already within India
A law under Article 2 is not treated as a constitutional amendment under Article 368
breakdown.how_to_read: Distinguish Article 2 (admitting/establishing States, typically involving territory not already part of India) from Article 3 (forming new States out of existing Indian territory) — the two are companion powers but operate on different starting points.

sections.title: [Sikkim to be associated with the Union.] Omitted
sections.raw_text: Omitted by the Constitution (Thirty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1975, s. 5 (w.e.f. 26-4-1975).

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 2A was inserted in 1975 to associate Sikkim with the Union of India as an 'Associate State' under a Tenth Schedule (the one now dealing with anti-defection is a different, later Tenth Schedule). Barely weeks later, Sikkim became a full State of India, so Article 2A and its associated Schedule were omitted altogether.
essential_elements: This is a numbering-only placeholder in the Constitution's article sequence
exceptions_and_qualifications: Superseded by the Constitution (Thirty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1975, which simultaneously inserted Sikkim as the 22nd State of India in the First Schedule and omitted Article 2A
breakdown.how_to_read: No independent legal content remains — Sikkim's actual constitutional status as a full State is now governed by its entry in the First Schedule read with Article 1, not by this omitted Article.

sections.title: Formation of new States and alteration of areas, boundaries or names of existing States
sections.raw_text: Parliament may by law— (a) form a new State by separation of territory from any State or by uniting two or more States or parts of States or by uniting any territory to a part of any State; (b) increase the area of any State; (c) diminish the area of any State; (d) alter the boundaries of any State; (e) alter the name of any State: Provided that no Bill for the purpose shall be introduced in either House of Parliament except on the recommendation of the President and unless, where the proposal contained in the Bill affects the area, boundaries or name of any of the States, the Bill has been referred by the President to the Legislature of that State for expressing its views thereon within such period as may be specified in the reference or within such further period as the President may allow and the period so specified or allowed has expired. Explanation I.—In this article, in clauses (a) to (e), 'State' includes a Union territory, but in the proviso, 'State' does not include a Union territory. Explanation II.—The power conferred on Parliament by clause (a) includes the power to form a new State or Union territory by uniting a part of any State or Union territory to any other State or Union territory.
key_terms: alteration of name of a State

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 3 is the engine that lets Parliament redraw India's internal map by ordinary law, without a constitutional amendment — carving new States out of existing ones, merging States, or simply resizing, reshaping, or renaming them. Because this power is so far-reaching, two safeguards apply: a Bill of this kind can only be introduced in Parliament on the President's recommendation, and if it touches a particular State's area, boundaries, or name, that State's own Legislature must first be given a chance to express its views (though Parliament is not bound by what the State says — it only has to consult, not obtain consent). The two Explanations clarify that 'State' in clauses (a)-(e) includes Union territories (so Union territories can also be reorganised this way), but for the consultation proviso specifically, 'State' excludes Union territories (so a Union territory's own 'legislature', where one exists, need not be consulted in the same mandatory way).
essential_elements: Parliament's law-making power covers forming new States, uniting States or parts of States, increasing or diminishing a State's area, altering boundaries, and altering names
A Bill can be introduced only on the President's prior recommendation
Where the Bill affects a specific State's area, boundaries, or name, that State's Legislature must be given an opportunity to express views within a period fixed by the President
'State' includes Union territories for the substantive powers in clauses (a)-(e), but excludes them for the mandatory-reference proviso
exceptions_and_qualifications: The State Legislature's views are only consultative — Parliament need not accept or even follow them
The time period for the State Legislature to respond can be extended by the President, and if the period lapses, Parliament may proceed regardless
Explanation II clarifies clause (a) extends to uniting parts of a State/Union territory with another State/Union territory, not just full States with each other
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the operative power behind every State reorganisation Act in Indian history (e.g., the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, and the bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh in 2014) — always check that a Presidential recommendation preceded introduction and that the affected State's Legislature was given a genuine opportunity to respond, since these are the key procedural safeguards courts have scrutinised.

sections.title: Laws made under articles 2 and 3 to provide for the amendment of the First and the Fourth Schedules and supplemental, incidental and consequential matters
sections.raw_text: (1) Any law referred to in article 2 or article 3 shall contain such provisions for the amendment of the First Schedule and the Fourth Schedule as may be necessary to give effect to the provisions of the law and may also contain such supplemental, incidental and consequential provisions (including provisions as to representation in Parliament and in the Legislature or Legislatures of the State or States affected by such law) as Parliament may deem necessary. (2) No such law as aforesaid shall be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of article 368.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 4 makes the Article 2/3 process self-contained: a law admitting, establishing, or reorganising States must itself update the First Schedule (list of States/territories) and the Fourth Schedule (allocation of Rajya Sabha seats to States), and may also make any other incidental adjustments Parliament thinks necessary — such as how many seats the affected State(s) get in Parliament or their own Legislature. Clause (2) is the crucial clarification: even though such a law changes parts of the Constitution's own Schedules, it is deliberately not treated as a 'constitutional amendment' requiring the special Article 368 procedure — ordinary legislative majority suffices.
essential_elements: A law under Article 2 or 3 must amend the First Schedule and Fourth Schedule as needed to give effect to it
It may also include supplemental, incidental, and consequential provisions, including on parliamentary/legislative representation
Such a law is expressly deemed NOT to be a constitutional amendment for Article 368 purposes
exceptions_and_qualifications: This exemption from Article 368 is precisely why State reorganisation can be done by simple parliamentary majority rather than the special amendment procedure (special majority, and for some subjects, State ratification)
breakdown.how_to_read: Article 4 is what makes Articles 2 and 3 practically usable as tools of ordinary politics rather than rare constitutional events — remember that any State reorganisation Bill is simultaneously a Schedule-amending Bill, and cite clause (2) whenever someone wrongly argues that a State reorganisation Act needed the Article 368 special procedure.

sections.title: Citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution
sections.raw_text: At the commencement of this Constitution, every person who has his domicile in the territory of India and— (a) who was born in the territory of India; or (b) either of whose parents was born in the territory of India; or (c) who has been ordinarily resident in the territory of India for not less than five years immediately preceding such commencement, shall be a citizen of India.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 5 is the Constitution's own 'starting gun' for Indian citizenship — it tells us who automatically became a citizen the moment the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950. The test has two parts: first, the person must have had their domicile (permanent home, in the legal sense) in India at that moment; second, they must satisfy at least one of three alternative conditions — being born in India, having a parent born in India, or having lived ordinarily in India for at least five years right before commencement.
essential_elements: Domicile in the territory of India at the commencement of the Constitution is the threshold requirement
At least one of three alternative conditions must additionally be satisfied: birth in India, parental birth in India, or five years' ordinary residence immediately before commencement
exceptions_and_qualifications: Article 5 only fixes citizenship as of the historical moment of commencement (26 January 1950) — citizenship acquired or lost afterward is governed by later law made under Article 11 (principally the Citizenship Act, 1955), not by this Article directly
Domicile is a distinct legal concept from mere residence or nationality, and its absence defeats the claim even if one of the three alternative conditions is met
breakdown.how_to_read: Use Article 5 only to determine 'origin-point' citizenship as of 26 January 1950 — for anyone born or naturalised after that date, or for loss/renunciation of citizenship at any time, go to the Citizenship Act, 1955 made under Article 11, not to this Article.

sections.title: Rights of citizenship of certain persons who have migrated to India from Pakistan
sections.raw_text: Notwithstanding anything in article 5, a person who has migrated to the territory of India from the territory now included in Pakistan shall be deemed to be a citizen of India at the commencement of this Constitution if— (a) he or either of his parents or any of his grand-parents was born in India as defined in the Government of India Act, 1935 (as originally enacted); and (b)(i) in the case where such person has so migrated before the nineteenth day of July, 1948, he has been ordinarily resident in the territory of India since the date of his migration, or (ii) in the case where such person has so migrated on or after the nineteenth day of July, 1948, he has been registered as a citizen of India by an officer appointed in that behalf by the Government of the Dominion of India on an application made by him therefor to such officer before the commencement of this Constitution in the form and manner prescribed by that Government: Provided that no person shall be so registered unless he has been resident in the territory of India for at least six months immediately preceding the date of his application.
key_terms: Government of India Act 1935 definition of India

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 6 deals with the enormous population movement of Partition, addressing people who migrated into India from what became Pakistan. It overrides the general Article 5 test with a special rule: such a migrant is deemed an Indian citizen at commencement if they (or a parent or grandparent) were born in undivided India as defined by the 1935 Government of India Act, AND they satisfy a time-based sub-test — if they migrated before 19 July 1948, simply having lived in India continuously since migrating suffices; but if they migrated on or after that date, they additionally needed to have formally registered as a citizen with a designated Dominion of India officer before the Constitution commenced, having been resident at least six months before applying.
essential_elements: Ancestral-birth condition: the person, a parent, or a grandparent must have been born in undivided India (1935 Act definition)
Time-split residence/registration condition depending on whether migration occurred before or on/after 19 July 1948
For post-19-July-1948 migrants, formal registration before commencement (preceded by at least six months' residence) was mandatory
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article operates 'notwithstanding' (overriding) Article 5 — it is a special deeming provision, not an application of the ordinary domicile-based test
The six-month residence proviso is a strict precondition to registration eligibility for the later category of migrants
breakdown.how_to_read: Article 6 is now almost entirely of historical/adjudicative interest for Partition-era migration disputes — read it together with Article 7 (the mirror-image provision for migrants going the other way) to see how the Constitution drew citizenship lines around the two-way Partition migration.

sections.title: Rights of citizenship of certain migrants to Pakistan
sections.raw_text: Notwithstanding anything in articles 5 and 6, a person who has after the first day of March, 1947, migrated from the territory of India to the territory now included in Pakistan shall not be deemed to be a citizen of India: Provided that nothing in this article shall apply to a person who, after having so migrated to the territory now included in Pakistan, has returned to the territory of India under a permit for resettlement or permanent return issued by or under the authority of any law and every such person shall for the purposes of clause (b) of article 6 be deemed to have migrated to the territory of India after the nineteenth day of July, 1948.
key_terms: permit for resettlement or permanent return

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 7 is the mirror image of Article 6: a person who migrated out of India, into what became Pakistan, after 1 March 1947, is treated as not an Indian citizen — even if they would otherwise qualify under Articles 5 or 6. There is, however, a return path: if such a person later came back to India under an official resettlement/permanent-return permit, they are not caught by this bar, and for the purposes of Article 6(b)'s registration rule, they are treated as if they had migrated into India only after 19 July 1948 (so they would need to have registered as a citizen, as Article 6 requires for that later category).
essential_elements: Base rule: migration out of India to Pakistan-territory after 1 March 1947 disqualifies a person from Indian citizenship under Articles 5/6
Proviso creates a return path via an official resettlement/permanent-return permit
A returnee under the proviso is deemed, for Article 6(b) purposes, to have migrated into India after 19 July 1948 — triggering the registration requirement
exceptions_and_qualifications: The bar in Article 7 overrides both Article 5 (the general test) and Article 6 (the migrant-into-India deeming rule) via its own non-obstante opening
The proviso's benefit is available only to those who returned under a lawful resettlement/permanent-return permit — informal or unauthorised return does not qualify
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Articles 6 and 7 as a linked pair governing Partition-era two-way migration — Article 6 deems certain in-migrants citizens, Article 7 deems certain out-migrants non-citizens, and the proviso to Article 7 is the narrow bridge back for people who left and then formally returned.

sections.title: Rights of citizenship of certain persons of Indian origin residing outside India
sections.raw_text: Notwithstanding anything in article 5, any person who or either of whose parents or any of whose grand-parents was born in India as defined in the Government of India Act, 1935 (as originally enacted), and who is ordinarily residing in any country outside India as so defined shall be deemed to be a citizen of India if he has been registered as a citizen of India by the diplomatic or consular representative of India in the country where he is for the time being residing on an application made by him therefor to such diplomatic or consular representative, whether before or after the commencement of this Constitution, in the form and manner prescribed by the Government of the Dominion of India or the Government of India.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 8 extends citizenship to the Indian diaspora of that era — people of Indian origin (by birth or ancestry, going back to a parent or grandparent) who were living abroad at the relevant time. Unlike Articles 5 and 6, which look at residence inside India, Article 8 lets such overseas persons become Indian citizens purely by registering with an Indian diplomatic or consular officer in the country where they were living, whether that registration happened before or after the Constitution commenced.
essential_elements: Ancestral-birth condition identical in structure to Article 6: self, parent, or grandparent born in undivided India
Ordinary residence in a country outside India (as defined by the 1935 Act) at the relevant time
Registration with an Indian diplomatic or consular representative abroad, in the prescribed form and manner, is the operative act that confers citizenship
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article, again, operates notwithstanding Article 5 — it is a distinct, self-contained route to citizenship for the overseas Indian-origin population, not an application of the domicile test
Registration could validly occur either before or after the Constitution's commencement — the timing itself is not fatal, unlike the stricter cut-off dates in Articles 6 and 7
breakdown.how_to_read: Do not confuse Article 8's diaspora-registration route (a one-time historical mechanism operating around commencement) with the modern Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) scheme, which is a creature of the Citizenship Act, 1955 as amended, made under Article 11.

sections.title: Persons voluntarily acquiring citizenship of a foreign State not to be citizens
sections.raw_text: No person shall be a citizen of India by virtue of article 5, or be deemed to be a citizen of India by virtue of article 6 or article 8, if he has voluntarily acquired the citizenship of any foreign State.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 9 enforces India's single-citizenship principle at the constitutional threshold: anyone who had voluntarily taken up the citizenship of another country is disqualified from being treated as an Indian citizen under Articles 5, 6, or 8, no matter how strong their birth or ancestral connection to India otherwise was.
essential_elements: Applies specifically to disqualify citizenship claims that would otherwise arise under Articles 5, 6, or 8
The acquisition of foreign citizenship must be voluntary — an involuntary or automatic conferral by foreign law (without the person's choice) would not trigger this bar in the same way
exceptions_and_qualifications: Article 9 does not itself regulate the loss of citizenship after a person has already become an Indian citizen and later acquires foreign citizenship — that is governed by the Citizenship Act, 1955 made under Article 11

Courts have had to interpret what counts as 'voluntary acquisition' in individual fact situations (e.g., automatic conferral of foreign nationality on marriage or by operation of foreign law without an affirmative act)
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat Article 9 as a threshold bar operating only at the Article 5/6/8 citizenship-determination stage — for citizenship already vested and later placed in doubt by acquisition of a foreign passport, the operative law is the Citizenship Act, 1955, not this Article directly.

sections.title: Continuance of the rights of citizenship
sections.raw_text: Every person who is or is deemed to be a citizen of India under any of the foregoing provisions of this Part shall, subject to the provisions of any law that may be made by Parliament, continue to be such citizen.
key_terms: subject to law made by Parliament

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 10 provides continuity: once a person qualifies as a citizen under any of Articles 5 to 9, that citizenship persists going forward, unless and until Parliament makes a law that changes the position (for instance, providing for loss of citizenship in specified circumstances).
essential_elements: Citizenship, once established under Articles 5-9, is presumed to continue indefinitely
This continuance is expressly made subject to future Parliamentary law — it is not an unconditional guarantee immune from legislative modification
exceptions_and_qualifications: The qualifying phrase 'subject to the provisions of any law that may be made by Parliament' is what allows the Citizenship Act, 1955 to validly provide for termination of citizenship (e.g., on voluntary acquisition of another citizenship, or by an order of the Central Government) without being unconstitutional
breakdown.how_to_read: Article 10 is the constitutional bridge that lets ordinary citizenship law override the default continuance rule — always check the Citizenship Act, 1955 (and its amendments) for whether a particular person's citizenship has since been terminated, rather than assuming permanence purely from satisfying Articles 5-9.

sections.title: Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law
sections.raw_text: Nothing in the foregoing provisions of this Part shall derogate from the power of Parliament to make any provision with respect to the acquisition and termination of citizenship and all other matters relating to citizenship.
key_terms: plenary power of Parliament over citizenship

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 11 is the Part's closing 'clear the decks' provision: it confirms that Articles 5 to 10 do not exhaust or limit Parliament's law-making power over citizenship. Parliament retains full authority to legislate on how citizenship is acquired (by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation) and how it is lost, and on any other citizenship-related matter — which is exactly the authority exercised through the Citizenship Act, 1955.
essential_elements: Parliament's power under Article 11 is plenary and not confined or cut down by the specific historical rules in Articles 5-10
Covers both acquisition and termination of citizenship, plus 'all other matters relating to citizenship'
exceptions_and_qualifications: Article 11 is what makes the Citizenship Act, 1955 (and later amendments such as those dealing with Overseas Citizens of India, or citizenship by registration/naturalisation) constitutionally valid — without this Article, Parliament's power might have been seen as limited to filling gaps left by Articles 5-10 rather than freely legislating the whole subject
breakdown.how_to_read: Whenever a citizenship question falls outside the narrow historical scenarios of Articles 5-9 (e.g., birth after 1950, naturalisation, or loss of citizenship), the governing law is legislation made by Parliament under this Article — principally the Citizenship Act, 1955 — not the constitutional Articles themselves.

sections.title: Definition
sections.raw_text: In this Part, unless the context otherwise requires, "the State" includes the Government and Parliament of India and the Government and the Legislature of each of the States and all local or other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India.
key_terms: under the control of the Government of India

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 12 answers a foundational question for the entire Fundamental Rights Part: against whom can these rights be enforced? It defines 'the State' broadly — not just the Union and State Governments and Legislatures, but also 'local or other authorities' operating within India or under Indian Government control. This wide definition determines which bodies (e.g., municipalities, statutory corporations, universities, regulatory authorities) can be sued for violating a fundamental right.
essential_elements: 'The State' expressly includes the Government and Parliament of India
It also includes the Government and Legislature of each State
It extends to all local authorities (e.g., municipalities, panchayats) and 'other authorities' within India or under Central Government control
exceptions_and_qualifications: Courts have developed tests (e.g., deep and pervasive State control, functional/financial dependence on government) to decide whether a particular body — such as a statutory corporation or a government company — qualifies as 'other authorities' and is therefore bound by Part III

Purely private individuals and private bodies not meeting these tests generally fall outside Article 12 and cannot be directly sued for fundamental rights violations (though some rights, like Article 17 and Article 23, expressly bind private persons too)
breakdown.how_to_read: Always check Article 12 first before invoking any fundamental right against a body other than the Union or a State Government directly — if the body is not 'the State' within this definition (as judicially elaborated), the fundamental-rights remedy under Article 32/226 may not be available against it at all.

sections.title: Laws inconsistent with or in derogation of the fundamental rights
sections.raw_text: (1) All laws in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution, in so far as they are inconsistent with the provisions of this Part, shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, be void. (2) The State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by this Part and any law made in contravention of this clause shall, to the extent of the contravention, be void. (3) In this article, unless the context otherwise requires,— (a) "law" includes any Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law; (b) "laws in force" includes laws passed or made by a Legislature or other competent authority in the territory of India before the commencement of this Constitution and not previously repealed, notwithstanding that any such law or any part thereof may not be then in operation either at all or in particular areas. (4) Nothing in this article shall apply to any amendment of this Constitution made under article 368.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 13 is the enforcement teeth of Part III: it makes both old (pre-1950) laws and any future law void to the extent they conflict with fundamental rights. Clause (1) strikes down pre-constitutional laws that clash with Part III (only to the extent of the conflict — the rest survives, per the doctrine of severability). Clause (2) is a forward-looking bar preventing the State from ever validly making a law that takes away or abridges a fundamental right; any such law is void to that extent. Clause (3) gives 'law' and 'laws in force' very wide definitions, sweeping in not just statutes but ordinances, rules, regulations, notifications, and even custom or usage having legal force. Clause (4), added later, clarifies that constitutional amendments made under Article 368 are not 'law' for Article 13 purposes — insulating amendments from being struck down merely for being inconsistent with a fundamental right (though the basic structure doctrine still constrains amendments through other means).
essential_elements: Clause (1): pre-constitutional inconsistent laws are void to the extent of inconsistency (not wholly void)
Clause (2): the State is barred from making any law that takes away or abridges Part III rights; violating laws are void to the extent of the contravention
Clause (3)(a)-(b): 'law' and 'laws in force' are defined expansively to include subordinate legislation and custom/usage with legal force
Clause (4): constitutional amendments under Article 368 are excluded from Article 13's reach
exceptions_and_qualifications: The doctrine of eclipse allows a pre-constitutional law inconsistent with a fundamental right to remain 'eclipsed' (dormant, unenforceable against citizens) rather than being wiped out entirely — it can revive if the relevant right is later amended away, though this doctrine is generally understood to apply differently to post-constitutional laws

Clause (4)'s exclusion of constitutional amendments does not mean amendments are wholly beyond judicial review — the basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati) independently limits Parliament's amending power under Article 368 itself
breakdown.how_to_read: Article 13 is the provision to cite whenever arguing that a statute, rule, notification, or even a custom is constitutionally void for violating a Part III right — but remember clause (4) means you cannot use Article 13 alone to challenge a constitutional amendment; for that, the basic structure doctrine under Article 368 jurisprudence is the relevant framework.

sections.title: Equality before law
sections.raw_text: The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 14 guarantees two related but distinct ideas to every person (not just citizens) within India: 'equality before the law' (a negative concept, borrowed from British constitutional tradition, meaning no one is above the law and all are equally subject to the ordinary law of the land) and 'equal protection of the laws' (a more positive, American-influenced concept, meaning like persons should be treated alike under the law). Together they form the bedrock non-discrimination guarantee of the Constitution, enforceable against 'the State' as defined in Article 12.
essential_elements: Applies to 'any person' — not limited to citizens, unlike some other Part III rights
'Equality before law' = no person is above the law; the law applies equally to all, including the State's own officials
'Equal protection of the laws' = persons in similar circumstances should be treated similarly, and the law itself must not be arbitrarily discriminatory
exceptions_and_qualifications: Article 14 does not forbid all classification by law — it only forbids 'class legislation' that is arbitrary; reasonable classification is permitted if it satisfies a twin test: (i) the classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia distinguishing grouped persons from others, and (ii) that differentia must have a rational nexus to the object sought to be achieved by the law

Article 14 has also been read (post-Maneka Gandhi and E.P. Royappa) to strike at arbitrariness itself — an arbitrary State action can violate Article 14 even without a classic 'classification' problem
breakdown.how_to_read: When pleading Article 14, always frame the argument through the two-limb reasonable-classification test (intelligible differentia + rational nexus) if challenging a classification, or through the broader 'arbitrariness' strand if challenging discretionary/arbitrary State action that doesn't fit the classification mould.

sections.title: Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth
sections.raw_text: (1) The State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them. (2) No citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them, be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition with regard to— (a) access to shops, public restaurants, hotels and places of public entertainment; or (b) the use of wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads and places of public resort maintained wholly or partly out of State funds or dedicated to the use of the general public. (3) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from making any special provision for women and children. (4) Nothing in this article or in clause (2) of article 29 shall prevent the State from making any special provision for the advancement of any socially and educationally backward classes of citizens or for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes. (5) Nothing in this article or in sub-clause (g) of clause (1) of article 19 shall prevent the State from making any special provision, by law, for the advancement of any socially and educationally backward classes of citizens or for the Scheduled Castes or the Scheduled Tribes in so far as such special provisions relate to their admission to educational institutions including private educational institutions, whether aided or unaided by the State, other than the minority educational institutions referred to in clause (1) of article 30. (6) Nothing in this article or sub-clause (g) of clause (1) of article 19 or clause (2) of article 29 shall prevent the State from making,— (a) any special provision for the advancement of any economically weaker sections of citizens other than the classes mentioned in clauses (4) and (5); and (b) any special provision for the advancement of any economically weaker sections of citizens other than the classes mentioned in clauses (4) and (5) in so far as such special provisions relate to their admission to educational institutions including private educational institutions, whether aided or unaided by the State, other than the minority educational institutions referred to in clause (1) of article 30, which in the case of reservation would be in addition to the existing reservations and subject to a maximum of ten per cent. of the total seats in each category. Explanation.—For the purposes of this article and article 16, "economically weaker sections" shall be such as may be notified by the State from time to time on the basis of family income and other indicators of economic disadvantage.
key_terms: grounds only of religion race caste sex place of birth
special provision for women and children

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 15 is Article 14's specific application against the historically most dangerous grounds of discrimination. Clauses (1)-(2) forbid the State (clause 1) and even private persons controlling public-facing establishments/resorts (clause 2) from discriminating against a citizen purely on religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. But the Article is equally famous for its enabling clauses: (3) permits affirmative special provisions for women and children; (4) and (5) permit reservations/special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes and for SCs/STs, including in educational institutions; and (6), added in 2019, extends similar (capped at 10%) affirmative provisions to economically weaker sections (EWS) not otherwise covered by (4)/(5), based on notified economic-disadvantage criteria.
essential_elements: Discrimination must be 'on grounds only of' the listed characteristics — if a classification uses an additional, non-listed factor together with a listed one, Article 15(1)/(2) is not automatically violated
Clause (2)'s prohibition on discriminatory access extends beyond the State to any establishment maintained wholly/partly from State funds or dedicated to public use
Clauses (3)-(6) are not exceptions carved out of a violation but express constitutional permissions ('nothing in this article shall prevent') for affirmative action
exceptions_and_qualifications: The EWS reservation under clause (6) is capped at a maximum of ten per cent and must be 'in addition to' existing reservations, and expressly excludes classes already covered by clauses (4) and (5)
Minority educational institutions referred to in Article 30(1) are excluded from the special educational-admission provisions in clauses (5) and (6)
breakdown.how_to_read: Distinguish the prohibitory clauses (1)-(2), which are the sword against discrimination, from the enabling clauses (3)-(6), which are shields protecting affirmative-action legislation from being struck down as reverse discrimination — a law under clause (4), (5), or (6) does not need to separately satisfy the Article 14 reasonable-classification test in the same way ordinary legislation does, because the Constitution itself has pre-authorised this category of classification.

sections.title: Equality of opportunity in matters of public employment
sections.raw_text: (1) There shall be equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State. (2) No citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them, be ineligible for, or discriminated against in respect of, any employment or office under the State. (3) Nothing in this article shall prevent Parliament from making any law prescribing, in regard to a class or classes of employment or appointment to an office under the Government of, or any local or other authority within, a State or Union territory, any requirement as to residence within that State or Union territory prior to such employment or appointment. (4) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from making any provision for the reservation of appointments or posts in favour of any backward class of citizens which, in the opinion of the State, is not adequately represented in the services under the State. (4A) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from making any provision for reservation in matters of promotion, with consequential seniority, to any class or classes of posts in the services under the State in favour of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes which, in the opinion of the State, are not adequately represented in the services under the State. (4B) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from considering any unfilled vacancies of a year which are reserved for being filled up in that year in accordance with any provision for reservation made under clause (4) or clause (4A) as a separate class of vacancies to be filled up in any succeeding year or years and such class of vacancies shall not be considered together with the vacancies of the year in which they are being filled up for determining the ceiling of fifty per cent. reservation on total number of vacancies of that year. (5) Nothing in this article shall affect the operation of any law which provides that the incumbent of an office in connection with the affairs of any religious or denominational institution or any member of the governing body thereof shall be a person professing a particular religion or belonging to a particular denomination. (6) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from making any provision for the reservation of appointments or posts in favour of any economically weaker sections of citizens other than the classes mentioned in clause (4), in addition to the existing reservation and subject to a maximum of ten per cent. of the posts in each category.
key_terms: equality of opportunity in public employment

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 16 applies the Article 14/15 equality principle specifically to jobs 'under the State' — government and public sector employment. Clause (1) guarantees equal opportunity; clause (2) forbids discrimination on the listed grounds (which here additionally include 'descent' and 'residence' beyond Article 15's list). The remaining clauses are the constitutional machinery for reservation policy in public employment: clause (3) lets Parliament impose State/UT residence requirements for certain posts; clause (4) permits reservation for backward classes inadequately represented in State services; (4A) extends this to promotions (with consequential seniority) for SCs/STs; (4B) allows unfilled reserved vacancies to be carried forward to future years without counting against the 50% ceiling for that later year; clause (5) preserves religious-denomination-based eligibility rules for offices tied to running religious institutions; and clause (6), added alongside Article 15(6), permits a further 10% EWS reservation.
essential_elements: Clause (1)-(2) establish the baseline: equal opportunity and non-discrimination on listed grounds in public employment
Clause (3) is the sole ground on which residence-based restriction is permitted, and only by Parliament's law, not State legislatures

Clauses (4), (4A), (4B), and (6) are successive enabling provisions permitting different forms of reservation, each with its own conditions (inadequate representation, promotion-specific consequential seniority, carry-forward treatment, and the EWS cap respectively)
exceptions_and_qualifications: The judicially evolved 50% ceiling on total reservations (from Indra Sawhant/Mandal jurisprudence) is not textually stated in Article 16 itself (except implicitly via clause 4B's cross-reference) but has been treated as a general limit, subject to the EWS clause (6) reservation being treated somewhat differently in recent jurisprudence
Clause (5)'s exception for denominational institution offices is narrow — confined to offices connected with the affairs of the religious/denominational institution itself
breakdown.how_to_read: When analysing a public employment reservation scheme, identify precisely which enabling clause it rests on — backward-class entry reservation (4), SC/ST promotion reservation (4A), carry-forward vacancy treatment (4B), or EWS reservation (6) — since each has distinct conditions and the 50% ceiling discourse applies differently to each.

sections.title: Abolition of Untouchability
sections.raw_text: "Untouchability" is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden. The enforcement of any disability arising out of "Untouchability" shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law.
key_terms: enforcement of disability arising out of Untouchability

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 17 is one of the few fundamental rights that operates directly against private individuals, not just the State. It abolishes the practice of 'Untouchability' in any form, and criminalises the enforcement of any disability that arises from it — meaning ordinary legislation (principally the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955, and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989) gives this constitutional abolition concrete penal teeth.
essential_elements: The abolition and prohibition operate horizontally — enforceable against private persons, not merely 'the State'

The Article itself does not define 'Untouchability' in detail (deliberately using the term in its historically understood, socially oppressive sense) or prescribe the specific punishment; both are left to ordinary law
exceptions_and_qualifications: Article 17's self-executing abolition is reinforced, not exhausted, by statutory law — the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 (originally the Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955) and later special legislation provide the actual offences and penalties contemplated by the phrase 'in accordance with law'
breakdown.how_to_read: Article 17 is a rare example of a fundamental right directly binding private citizens — when a discrimination claim arises from caste-based social exclusion practised by private individuals (not the State), this is the Article to invoke, read together with the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955.

sections.title: Abolition of titles
sections.raw_text: (1) No title, not being a military or academic distinction, shall be conferred by the State. (2) No citizen of India shall accept any title from any foreign State. (3) No person who is not a citizen of India shall, while he holds any office of profit or trust under the State, accept without the consent of the President any title from any foreign State. (4) No person holding any office of profit or trust under the State shall, without the consent of the President, accept any present, emolument, or office of any kind from or under any foreign State.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 18 reflects the framers' rejection of hereditary/feudal titles (like the colonial-era 'Rai Bahadur' or 'Sir') as instruments of State-conferred hierarchy. Clause (1) bars the Indian State itself from conferring such titles, while carving out ordinary military and academic distinctions (e.g., gallantry awards, degrees). Clauses (2)-(4) then guard against foreign entanglement and undue influence: citizens cannot accept titles from foreign States at all; non-citizens holding a State office of profit/trust need presidential consent to accept a foreign title; and anyone holding such a State office needs presidential consent even to accept a foreign present, payment, or office.
essential_elements: Clause (1): the State cannot confer non-military, non-academic titles — this is what underlies the National Awards (Bharat Ratna, Padma awards) being formally styled as non-titular civilian 'awards' or 'distinctions', not titles, following constitutional and judicial clarification (Balaji Raghavan case)
Clauses (2)-(4) form an escalating scheme regulating foreign honours/benefits based on citizenship and whether the recipient holds a State office of profit or trust
exceptions_and_qualifications: Military and academic distinctions are expressly excluded from clause (1)'s bar and may be freely conferred by the State
Presidential consent under clauses (3) and (4) is a case-specific safeguard, not a blanket permission — each acceptance requires its own consent
breakdown.how_to_read: Cite Article 18 whenever a dispute involves the constitutionality of State-conferred honours (distinguishing genuine 'titles' from permitted awards/distinctions) or a foreign-honours-acceptance controversy involving a public office-holder — the operative question is always whether presidential consent under clauses (3)/(4) was sought where required.

sections.title: Protection of certain rights regarding freedom of speech, etc.
sections.raw_text: (1) All citizens shall have the right— (a) to freedom of speech and expression; (b) to assemble peaceably and without arms; (c) to form associations or unions or co-operative societies; (d) to move freely throughout the territory of India; (e) to reside and settle in any part of the territory of India; and (g) to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business. (2) Nothing in sub-clause (a) of clause (1) shall affect the operation of any existing law, or prevent the State from making any law, in so far as such law imposes reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the said sub-clause in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, or in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence. (3) Nothing in sub-clause (b) of the said clause shall affect the operation of any existing law in so far as it imposes, or prevent the State from making any law imposing, in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India or public order, reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the said sub-clause. (4) Nothing in sub-clause (c) of the said clause shall affect the operation of any existing law in so far as it imposes, or prevent the State from making any law imposing, in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India or public order or morality, reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the said sub-clause.
