(2) It shall be the duty of the Attorney-General to give advice to the Government of India upon such legal matters, and to perform such other duties of a legal character, as may from time to time be referred or assigned to him by the President, and to discharge the functions conferred on him by or under this Constitution or any other law for the time being in force.
(3) In the performance of his duties the Attorney-General shall have right of audience in all courts in the territory of India.
(4) The Attorney-General shall hold office during the pleasure of the President, and shall receive such remuneration as the President may determine.
key_terms: qualified to be a Supreme Court Judge (Attorney-General)
right of audience in all courts

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 76 creates the office of Attorney-General for India — the Union Government's chief law officer — appointed by the President from among persons qualified to be Supreme Court Judges (the same qualification bar as a sitting Judge, though the Attorney-General is not a Judge). The Attorney-General advises the Government on legal matters, performs other legal duties assigned by the President or by law, enjoys the right to appear in any court in India, and holds office at the President's pleasure with remuneration the President determines.
essential_elements: Clause (1): appointment qualification is 'qualified to be appointed a Judge of the Supreme Court' — i.e., the Article 124(3) qualifications (citizenship, and either five years as a High Court Judge, or ten years as a High Court advocate, or the President's opinion of being a distinguished jurist), appointed by the President.

Clause (2): the Attorney-General's core duty is to advise the Government of India on legal matters and perform other legal-character duties referred by the President, plus any functions conferred by the Constitution or other law (e.g., appearing in certain constitutionally mandated proceedings).

Clause (3): right of audience in all courts in India — the Attorney-General may appear and be heard in any court in the country, unlike ordinary counsel who must be enrolled/entitled to practice in a particular court.
Clause (4): tenure is 'during the pleasure of the President' (no fixed term specified in the text), and remuneration is fixed by the President rather than by a Schedule or Parliamentary law.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Unlike the Comptroller and Auditor-General (Article 148) or Election Commissioners, the Attorney-General has no security-of-tenure protection or fixed term written into the article — the office is explicitly tenure-at-pleasure, reflecting its character as the Government's own legal adviser rather than an independent constitutional check.

The Attorney-General is not a full-time civil servant and is constitutionally permitted to maintain private legal practice, subject to conventions/restrictions on not appearing against the Government of India — a convention-based limit rather than an Article 76 textual restriction.

Clause (3)'s 'right of audience in all courts' is a privilege of appearance, not a grant of any additional judicial or quasi-judicial power — it does not make the Attorney-General a court officer with independent authority.
breakdown.how_to_read: Contrast the Attorney-General's pleasure-tenure, advisory role under Article 76 against the security-of-tenure enjoyed by judicial and quasi-judicial constitutional officers (Supreme Court Judges under Article 124, CAG under Article 148) — the difference in tenure protection tracks the difference in institutional role (Government's counsel vs. independent constitutional authority).

sections.title: Conduct of business of the Government of India
sections.raw_text:
77. Conduct of business of the Government of India.—(1) All executive action of the Government of India shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the President.
(2) Orders and other instruments made and executed in the name of the President shall be authenticated in such manner as may be specified in rules to be made by the President, and the validity of an order or instrument which is so authenticated shall not be called in question on the ground that it is not an order or instrument made or executed by the President.
(3) The President shall make rules for the more convenient transaction of the business of the Government of India, and for the allocation among Ministers of the said business.
key_terms: executive action taken in the name of the President

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 77 supplies the formal machinery through which the Article 53/74 principle (executive power vested in a President who acts on ministerial advice) plays out on paper: every act of the Union Government is formally expressed as done in the President's name, authenticated per rules the President makes, with authenticated orders immune from challenge merely on the ground they weren't personally made by the President — and the President also makes the 'Rules of Business' that allocate government work among Ministers and departments.
essential_elements: Clause (1): all Union executive action must be formally expressed as taken in the name of the President, regardless of which Minister or official actually decided it — the constitutional fiction that makes the President the nominal author of all government action.

Clause (2): orders/instruments made in the President's name must be authenticated per rules the President prescribes; once so authenticated, their validity cannot be questioned merely on the ground that they weren't actually made or executed by the President personally — protecting administrative action from a purely formal attack.
Clause (3): the President makes 'Rules of Business' governing the convenient transaction of Government of India business and the allocation of that business among the various Ministers/Ministries.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (2)'s immunity from challenge is limited to the specific ground that the order wasn't personally made by the President — it does not immunise an order from substantive challenge on other grounds (illegality, lack of authority, violation of rights, etc.).

The Rules of Business made under clause (3) are themselves made by the President formally, but as with all Article 74-governed action, in substance on the advice of the Council of Ministers — they are not the President's independent policy choice.

A once-inserted clause (4) — added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) to require the Prime Minister to furnish information to the President if required — was subsequently omitted by the 44th Amendment (1978); its substance survives instead in the freestanding Article 78(b), reflecting a deliberate post-Emergency restructuring rather than an accidental gap.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 77 as the paperwork counterpart to Article 74's substantive rule — Article 74 says the President must act on ministerial advice, and Article 77 explains how that advice-driven action gets formally documented, authenticated, and allocated among Ministries via the Rules of Business.

sections.title: Duties of Prime Minister as respects the furnishing of information to the President, etc.
sections.raw_text:
78. Duties of Prime Minister as respects the furnishing of information to the President, etc.—It shall be the duty of the Prime Minister—
(a) to communicate to the President all decisions of the Council of Ministers relating to the administration of the affairs of the Union and proposals for legislation;
(b) to furnish such information relating to the administration of the affairs of the Union and proposals for legislation as the President may call for; and
(c) if the President so requires, to submit for the consideration of the Council of Ministers any matter on which a decision has been taken by a Minister but which has not been considered by the Council.
key_terms: Prime Minister's duty to communicate Council decisions
President's power to call for information
individual Minister decision referred to full Council

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 78 is the President's information channel into Cabinet government, running through the Prime Minister as the sole conduit: the PM must proactively report all Council of Ministers decisions on Union administration and legislative proposals, must supply further information the President calls for, and — if the President so requires — must place before the full Council any matter an individual Minister decided alone without the Council's collective consideration, preserving the President's (and thereby the Council's own collective-responsibility) oversight of decisions taken outside full Cabinet deliberation.
essential_elements: Clause (a): the Prime Minister must communicate to the President every Council of Ministers decision relating to Union administration and every legislative proposal — an affirmative, ongoing reporting duty, not merely a response-on-request obligation.
Clause (b): the Prime Minister must furnish whatever further information on Union administration or legislative proposals the President specifically calls for.

Clause (c): if the President requires it, the Prime Minister must place before the full Council of Ministers, for its consideration, any matter that an individual Minister decided on their own without the Council having considered it.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (c) operates only 'if the President so requires' — it is not automatic; the President must actively invoke it to pull an individual ministerial decision back to full Council scrutiny.

This article gives the President a channel for information and a mechanism to insist on collective consideration, but does not give the President any independent power to overrule or veto the resulting Cabinet decision — that remains governed by Article 74's binding-advice rule.

The substance of what became Article 78(b) had briefly existed as Article 77(4) (inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976) before being omitted by the 44th Amendment (1978) and effectively relocated/preserved in this freestanding Article 78 duty on the Prime Minister.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Articles 74, 77, and 78 as one connected sequence: Article 74 establishes the President must act on Cabinet advice; Article 77 formalises how that advice becomes documented executive action; Article 78 ensures the President is actually kept informed of Cabinet decisions and proposals so the Article 74 advisory relationship functions in substance, not just on paper — this closes out Chapter I of Part V before Chapter II (Parliament) begins at Article 79.

sections.title: Constitution of Parliament
sections.raw_text: 79. Constitution of Parliament.—There shall be a Parliament for the Union which shall consist of the President and two Houses to be known respectively as the Council of States and the House of the People.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 79 is the founding declaration of India's Union legislature: Parliament is not just the two Houses but a three-part institution comprising the President plus the Council of States (Rajya Sabha, the upper House) and the House of the People (Lok Sabha, the lower House) — a structural point that matters because a Bill only becomes law after passing both Houses and receiving the President's assent under Article 111, making the President legally part of 'Parliament' even though not a member of either House.
essential_elements: Parliament consists of three components: the President, the Council of States, and the House of the People.
The Council of States (Rajya Sabha) is the upper House, representing the States and Union territories.
The House of the People (Lok Sabha) is the lower House, representing the people through direct election.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The President is part of 'Parliament' for constitutional purposes (e.g., assent to Bills under Article 111, summoning/proroguing sessions under Article 85) but is not a 'member' of either House and does not sit or vote in either House's proceedings.

This bicameral-plus-President structure is fixed by this article for the Union; individual States are not required to have two Houses (see Article 168, which makes a State's Legislative Council optional).
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat Article 79 as the opening frame for all of Chapter II — every subsequent article (composition of each House, duration, qualifications, officers, procedure, legislative process in Chapter III) elaborates on this basic three-part structure.

sections.title: Composition of the Council of States
sections.raw_text:
80. Composition of the Council of States.—(1) The Council of States shall consist of—
(a) twelve members to be nominated by the President in accordance with the provisions of clause (3); and
(b) not more than two hundred and thirty-eight representatives of the States and of the Union territories.
(2) The allocation of seats in the Council of States to be filled by representatives of the States and of the Union territories shall be in accordance with the provisions in that behalf contained in the Fourth Schedule.
(3) The members to be nominated by the President under sub-clause (a) of clause (1) shall consist of persons having special knowledge or practical experience in respect of such matters as the following, namely:— Literature, science, art and social service.
(4) The representatives of each State in the Council of States shall be elected by the elected members of the Legislative Assembly of the State in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote.
(5) The representatives of the Union territories in the Council of States shall be chosen in such manner as Parliament may by law prescribe.
key_terms: nominated members of the Council of States
special knowledge or practical experience (Rajya Sabha nominees)
indirect election of Rajya Sabha members

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 80 fixes the Rajya Sabha's composition: up to 238 elected representatives of States and Union territories (seat numbers per State fixed in the Fourth Schedule) plus 12 members nominated by the President specifically for their distinction in literature, science, art, or social service — giving the House a built-in channel for expertise not tied to electoral politics. State representatives are chosen indirectly, by the State's own elected Assembly members using proportional representation by single transferable vote (the same method used for Presidential elections under Article 55), while Union territory representatives are chosen however Parliament prescribes by law.
essential_elements: Clause (1)(a): 12 members nominated by the President for special knowledge/practical experience in literature, science, art, or social service (the 'nominated members').
Clause (1)(b): not more than 238 elected representatives of the States and Union territories combined.
Clause (2): the actual State-by-State/UT-by-UT seat allocation is fixed in the Fourth Schedule, not in this article itself.
Clause (3): specifies the four categories of distinction qualifying a person for Presidential nomination.

Clause (4): State representatives are elected indirectly by the elected members of that State's Legislative Assembly, using proportional representation by single transferable vote — not by the general public directly.
Clause (5): Union territory representatives are chosen by whatever method Parliament prescribes by law (since most UTs lack a full Legislative Assembly).
exceptions_and_qualifications: Only the elected (not nominated) members of a State Legislative Assembly vote for that State's Rajya Sabha representatives under clause (4) — nominated Assembly members are excluded from this electorate, paralleling the Article 54 Presidential-electoral-college rule.

Nominated members under clause (1)(a) are chosen entirely on the President's (i.e., Union Council of Ministers') assessment of distinction in the four listed fields — there is no electorate for these 12 seats at all.
The 238-seat cap in clause (1)(b) is a ceiling ('not more than'), with the Fourth Schedule's actual allocation periodically amended by Parliament as States/UTs are reorganised.
breakdown.how_to_read: Cross-reference the Fourth Schedule for the actual per-State/UT seat numbers, and compare clause (4)'s single-transferable-vote method against Article 55(3)'s identical method for Presidential elections — both use PR-STV precisely because they are indirect elections by a defined body of electors rather than direct mass elections.

sections.title: Composition of the House of the People
sections.raw_text:
81. Composition of the House of the People.—(1) Subject to the provisions of article 331, the House of the People shall consist of—
(a) not more than five hundred and thirty members chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies in the States, and
(b) not more than twenty members to represent the Union territories, chosen in such manner as Parliament may by law provide.
(2) For the purposes of sub-clause (a) of clause (1),—
(a) there shall be allotted to each State a number of seats in the House of the People in such manner that the ratio between that number and the population of the State is, so far as practicable, the same for all States; and
(b) each State shall be divided into territorial constituencies in such manner that the ratio between the population of each constituency and the number of seats allotted to it is, so far as practicable, the same throughout the State:
Provided that the provisions of sub-clause (a) of this clause shall not be applicable for the purpose of allotment of seats in the House of the People to any State so long as the population of that State does not exceed six millions.
(3) In this article, the expression 'population' means the population as ascertained at the last preceding census of which the relevant figures have been published:
Provided that the reference in this clause to the last preceding census of which the relevant figures have been published shall, until the relevant figures for the first census taken after the year 2026 have been published, be construed,—
(i) for the purposes of sub-clause (a) of clause (2) and the proviso to that clause, as a reference to the 1971 census; and
(ii) for the purposes of sub-clause (b) of clause (2) as a reference to the 2001 census.
key_terms: direct election to the House of the People
five hundred and thirty members cap (Lok Sabha)
State-wise seat allocation by population ratio
population for Lok Sabha allocation (1971/2001 census freeze)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 81 fixes the Lok Sabha's composition: up to 530 members directly elected from State territorial constituencies plus up to 20 representing Union territories, with the guiding principle that seats-per-State and constituency sizes-within-a-State should track population as closely as practicable — except that, exactly like Article 55's Presidential electoral college, the population figures used are frozen (1971 census for State-wise seat allocation, 2001 census for intra-State constituency delimitation) until the first census after 2026 is published, so that States which controlled population growth are not penalized with proportionally fewer seats relative to faster-growing States.
essential_elements: Clause (1)(a): up to 530 members directly elected from territorial constituencies within the States.
Clause (1)(b): up to 20 members representing Union territories, chosen by whatever method Parliament prescribes by law.
Clause (2)(a): seats are allotted among States so that the seats-to-population ratio is, as far as practicable, uniform across all States.
Clause (2)(b): within a State, constituencies are drawn so that the population-per-seat ratio is, as far as practicable, uniform throughout that State.
Proviso to clause (2): the population-ratio allotment rule under (2)(a) does not apply to any State with a population of six million or less.

Clause (3) and its proviso: 'population' means the last published census figures, but this is frozen — 1971 census for inter-State seat allocation, 2001 census for intra-State constituency delimitation — until the first census after 2026 is published.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The population freeze is a deliberate, temporary policy choice (originally tied to 2000, then extended via the 84th and 87th Amendments to 2026) designed to avoid rewarding States with higher population growth with more parliamentary seats, not an oversight or permanent rule.
The six-million-population proviso in clause (2) exempts smaller States from the strict seats-to-population ratio rule, protecting their minimum representation regardless of population size.
This article's 530-seat cap and delimitation machinery interact directly with Article 82 (readjustment after each census), which governs when and how the actual redrawing of constituencies happens.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read this alongside Article 82 (readjustment after census) and the Article 55 Explanation (identical population-freeze technique for the Presidential electoral college) — both provisions use the same 1971/2026 freeze mechanism for the same underlying policy reason.

sections.title: Readjustment after each census
sections.raw_text:
82. Readjustment after each census.—Upon the completion of each census, the allocation of seats in the House of the People to the States and the division of each State into territorial constituencies shall be readjusted by such authority and in such manner as Parliament may by law determine:
Provided that such readjustment shall not affect representation in the House of the People until the dissolution of the then existing House:
Provided further that such readjustment shall take effect from such date as the President may, by order, specify and until such readjustment takes effect, any election to the House may be held on the basis of the territorial constituencies existing before such readjustment:
Provided also that until the relevant figures for the first census taken after the year 2026 have been published, it shall not be necessary to readjust—
(i) the allocation of seats in the House of the People to the States as readjusted on the basis of the 1971 census; and
(ii) the division of each State into territorial constituencies as may be readjusted on the basis of the 2001 census,
under this article.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 82 is the machinery provision implementing Article 81's population-ratio principle over time: after every census, Parliament (in practice, via a Delimitation Commission it establishes by law) must readjust both the State-wise seat allocation and the intra-State constituency boundaries — but any such readjustment only takes effect for the next general election (the sitting House is never disturbed mid-term), and, mirroring Article 81's freeze, no fresh readjustment has been required since the 1971/2001-based delimitation until the first census after 2026.
essential_elements: Main clause: after each census, seat allocation to States and constituency boundaries within States must be readjusted by whatever authority and method Parliament fixes by law (historically, a Delimitation Commission).
First proviso: readjustment does not affect the composition or representation of the currently sitting House of the People — it only applies from the next dissolution onward.
Second proviso: readjustment takes effect from a date the President specifies by order, and elections held before that date use the pre-existing constituencies.

Third proviso: no fresh readjustment is required under this article until the first census after 2026 is published — the current delimitation (1971 census basis for inter-State allocation, 2001 census basis for intra-State boundaries) remains frozen until then.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The freeze under the third proviso does not repeal the readjustment obligation permanently — it merely suspends the obligation until the post-2026 census, at which point full readjustment under the main clause and Article 81(2) resumes in the ordinary course.

The first proviso's protection of the sitting House means even a controversial or overdue delimitation exercise cannot be used to unseat or reconstitute a currently sitting Lok Sabha before its term naturally ends.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read this as Article 81's operational twin — Article 81 states the population-ratio principle and defines 'population' (with its own freeze), while Article 82 is the procedural article that actually triggers periodic delimitation exercises and carries the parallel freeze for the readjustment process itself.

sections.title: Duration of Houses of Parliament
sections.raw_text:
83. Duration of Houses of Parliament.—(1) The Council of States shall not be subject to dissolution, but as nearly as possible one-third of the members thereof shall retire as soon as may be on the expiration of every second year in accordance with the provisions made in that behalf by Parliament by law.
(2) The House of the People, unless sooner dissolved, shall continue for five years from the date appointed for its first meeting and no longer and the expiration of the said period of five years shall operate as a dissolution of the House:
Provided that the said period may, while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, be extended by Parliament by law for a period not exceeding one year at a time and not extending in any case beyond a period of six months after the Proclamation has ceased to operate.
key_terms: Council of States is a permanent body
one-third retirement every two years (Rajya Sabha)
five-year term of the House of the People
Emergency extension of Lok Sabha term

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 83 captures the fundamental structural difference between India's two Houses: the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) is a permanent body that is never dissolved, with roughly one-third of its members retiring every two years on a rotating basis (giving it institutional continuity), while the Lok Sabha (House of the People) has a fixed five-year term from its first sitting and automatically dissolves at the end of that term unless dissolved earlier — with the sole exception that Parliament can extend the Lok Sabha's term by up to one year at a time during a Proclamation of Emergency, subject to an outer limit of six months after the Emergency ends.
essential_elements: Clause (1): the Council of States is permanent (never dissolved as a body); approximately one-third of its members retire every two years per rules Parliament makes by law — this is the origin of the Rajya Sabha's staggered/rotating membership.
Clause (2) main text: the House of the People's term is five years from the date of its first meeting, after which it automatically dissolves unless dissolved earlier by the President.

Proviso to clause (2): during a Proclamation of Emergency, Parliament may extend the Lok Sabha's term by law, in increments of up to one year at a time, but never beyond six months after the Emergency ceases to operate.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The five-year term figure itself has been amended twice in history — extended to six years by the 42nd Amendment (1976) during the Emergency, then restored to five years by the 44th Amendment (1978) — a fact often tested as an example of Emergency-era overreach and subsequent correction.

The Emergency-extension proviso is the only textual mechanism for extending the Lok Sabha beyond five years; it cannot be extended by ordinary law absent an operating Proclamation of Emergency under Article 352.
'As nearly as possible one-third' in clause (1) is a practical approximation, not a mathematically exact fraction, reflecting real-world constraints in staggering retirements evenly.
breakdown.how_to_read: Contrast this directly against the President's and Vice-President's fixed five-year terms with hold-over provisos (Articles 56, 67) — the Lok Sabha's term is similarly five years but is a House-dissolution event rather than an individual office-holder's tenure, and only the Lok Sabha (not the permanent Rajya Sabha) has a 'duration' in this sense at all.

sections.title: Qualification for membership of Parliament
sections.raw_text:
84. Qualification for membership of Parliament.—A person shall not be qualified to be chosen to fill a seat in Parliament unless he—
(a) is a citizen of India, and makes and subscribes before some person authorised in that behalf by the Election Commission an oath or affirmation according to the form set out for the purpose in the Third Schedule;
(b) is, in the case of a seat in the Council of States, not less than thirty years of age and, in the case of a seat in the House of the People, not less than twenty-five years of age; and
(c) possesses such other qualifications as may be prescribed in that behalf by or under any law made by Parliament.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 84 lists the three baseline qualifications a person must meet to be chosen to Parliament: Indian citizenship plus a pre-candidacy oath/affirmation before an Election Commission-authorised person, a minimum age that differs by House (30 for Rajya Sabha, 25 for Lok Sabha, reflecting the upper House's traditionally more senior/deliberative character), and any further qualifications Parliament chooses to prescribe by ordinary law (the vehicle for this being the Representation of the People Act, 1951).
essential_elements: Clause (a): Indian citizenship, plus making and subscribing the prescribed Third Schedule oath/affirmation before a person the Election Commission authorises, before the candidacy formally proceeds.
Clause (b): minimum age of 30 years for a Council of States (Rajya Sabha) seat, and 25 years for a House of the People (Lok Sabha) seat — a differentiated age threshold between the two Houses.
Clause (c): Parliament may by ordinary law prescribe additional qualifications beyond citizenship, oath, and age.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (a)'s pre-candidacy oath under Article 84 is distinct from the Article 99 oath every member takes before actually taking their seat after being elected — the Article 84 oath is a candidacy prerequisite, the Article 99 oath is a post-election formality before sitting.

Clause (c) delegates open-ended power to Parliament to add qualifications by ordinary legislation — most notably exercised through the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (e.g., electoral roll enrolment requirements).
The age differential in clause (b) is a deliberate design choice mirroring many bicameral systems' convention of a higher minimum age for the upper, more deliberative House.
breakdown.how_to_read: Compare this to Article 173 (the parallel qualification article for State Legislature membership) — the structure (citizenship/oath, differentiated age by House, residual Parliament-prescribed qualifications) is essentially mirrored at the State level.

sections.title: Sessions of Parliament, prorogation and dissolution
sections.raw_text:
85. Sessions of Parliament, prorogation and dissolution.—(1) The President shall from time to time summon each House of Parliament to meet at such time and place as he thinks fit, but six months shall not intervene between its last sitting in one session and the date appointed for its first sitting in the next session.
(2) The President may from time to time—
(a) prorogue the Houses or either House;
(b) dissolve the House of the People.
key_terms: dissolution of the House of the People (Presidential power)

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 85 gives the President (acting, per Article 74, on ministerial advice) the formal power to summon Parliament into session, subject to a hard outer limit — no more than six months may elapse between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next, guaranteeing Parliament meets at least twice a year — and separately the power to prorogue (formally end a session without dissolving the House) or, for the Lok Sabha specifically, to dissolve the House altogether.
essential_elements: Clause (1): the President summons each House to meet, at a time and place of the President's choosing, subject to the mandatory six-month maximum gap between sessions.
Clause (2)(a): the President may prorogue (bring a session to a formal close, without ending the House's five-year term) either House or both.
Clause (2)(b): the President may dissolve the House of the People specifically — the Council of States, being permanent under Article 83(1), cannot be dissolved.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The six-month rule is a floor on frequency, not a fixed calendar — Parliament may (and does) meet more often than the minimum required; it only guarantees sessions are never spaced more than six months apart.

Prorogation and dissolution are distinct: prorogation ends only the current session (bills pending in a House generally survive prorogation, subject to specific rules on pending business), while dissolution ends the House of the People's very existence, requiring fresh general elections.

As with all Presidential functions, summoning, proroguing, and dissolving are formally the President's acts but are, per Article 74, exercised on the binding advice of the Council of Ministers (in practice, chiefly the Prime Minister's advice for dissolution).
breakdown.how_to_read: Read the six-month rule together with Article 83 (Lok Sabha's five-year term) and Article 356/352 (Emergency powers) for the full picture of how often, and under what circumstances outside the ordinary term, Parliament convenes or is dissolved.

sections.title: Right of President to address and send messages to Houses
sections.raw_text:
86. Right of President to address and send messages to Houses.—(1) The President may address either House of Parliament or both Houses assembled together, and for that purpose require the attendance of members.
(2) The President may send messages to either House of Parliament, whether with respect to a Bill then pending in Parliament or otherwise, and a House to which any message is so sent shall with all convenient despatch consider any matter required by the message to be taken into consideration.
key_terms: President's power to send messages to Houses

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 86 gives the President two distinct communication channels into Parliament, separate from the mandatory annual address under Article 87: a general right to address either or both Houses on any occasion (with power to compel members' attendance for that address), and a right to send written messages to either House on any matter, whether or not a Bill is pending, which obliges that House to take up the message's subject with all convenient despatch.
essential_elements: Clause (1): the President may address either House individually, or both Houses assembled together, and may require members to attend for that purpose.
Clause (2): the President may send messages to either House on any matter (Bill-related or otherwise), and the receiving House must consider the message's subject with all convenient despatch.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This general address/message power under Article 86 is distinct from, and in addition to, the mandatory special address at the start of each year and after each general election under Article 87 — Article 86 is discretionary and occasion-specific, Article 87 is a fixed annual/post-election obligation.
'With all convenient despatch' in clause (2) imposes a duty of prompt consideration on the receiving House but does not fix a specific timeline or guarantee any particular legislative outcome.
breakdown.how_to_read: Distinguish clearly from Article 87 (the mandatory special address) — Article 86 is the President's general, discretionary communication power, exercised (like all Presidential functions) on Council of Ministers advice under Article 74.

sections.title: Special address by the President
sections.raw_text:
87. Special address by the President.—(1) At the commencement of the first session after each general election to the House of the People and at the commencement of the first session of each year the President shall address both Houses of Parliament assembled together and inform Parliament of the causes of its summons.
(2) Provision shall be made by the rules regulating the procedure of either House for the allotment of time for discussion of the matters referred to in such address.
key_terms: commencement of first session after general election
commencement of first session of each year

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 87 makes the President's address to Parliament mandatory (unlike the discretionary Article 86 address) on two specific occasions: the opening of the first session after every fresh general election to the Lok Sabha, and the opening of the first session of every calendar year — informing Parliament, in each case, of the reasons for its summons (in practice, the Government's legislative and policy agenda). Each House's own procedural rules must allot dedicated time to discuss the matters raised in that address.
essential_elements: Clause (1): the President must address both Houses assembled together at two mandatory points — the first session after each general election, and the first session of each year — informing Parliament of the causes of its summons.
Clause (2): each House's procedural rules must set aside time specifically to discuss the matters covered in the special address.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This mandatory address is popularly known as the 'President's Address' (often reported as an annual event) and, in substance, is drafted by the Council of Ministers (per Article 74) even though delivered by the President personally — it sets out the government's legislative programme rather than the President's independent views.

A discussion on the President's Address (the 'Motion of Thanks') is a significant parliamentary event precisely because clause (2) mandates dedicated debate time on it, distinguishing it from an ordinary discretionary Article 86 address which carries no such guaranteed discussion time.
breakdown.how_to_read: Pair this with Article 86 for the full picture of Presidential communication with Parliament — Article 87 is the mandatory, twice-triggered 'State of the Union'-style address with guaranteed debate time, while Article 86 is the residual discretionary power for any other occasion.

sections.title: Rights of Ministers and Attorney-General as respects Houses
sections.raw_text: 88. Rights of Ministers and Attorney-General as respects Houses.—Every Minister and the Attorney-General of India shall have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, either House, any joint sitting of the Houses, and any committee of Parliament of which he may be named a member, but shall not by virtue of this article be entitled to vote.
key_terms: Ministers' right to speak in either House
Attorney-General's right to speak in Parliament
no voting right by virtue of Article 88

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 88 solves a practical problem created by India's parliamentary system: a Minister who is a member of the Rajya Sabha needs to be able to participate in Lok Sabha proceedings (and vice versa), and the Attorney-General — not an elected member of either House at all — still needs a voice in Parliament to advise on legal matters and defend government legislation. This article grants both categories a right to speak and otherwise participate in either House, any joint sitting, and any Parliamentary committee they're named to, but explicitly withholds any voting right that this article alone would otherwise confer.
essential_elements: Covers two categories: every Minister (regardless of which House, if any, they belong to) and the Attorney-General of India.
Grants the right to speak in, and otherwise participate in the proceedings of, either House, any joint sitting of the Houses, and any Parliamentary committee of which the person is named a member.
Expressly denies any voting right arising 'by virtue of this article' — participation rights and voting rights are kept strictly separate.
exceptions_and_qualifications: A Minister who happens to actually be an elected/nominated member of a particular House retains their ordinary voting right in that House as a member — Article 88 only clarifies they get no additional voting right in the other House (or elsewhere) merely by virtue of being a Minister; the Attorney-General, never being a member of either House, has no voting right anywhere under this article.

This is the same underlying rationale — allowing informed participation without conferring representative legitimacy through a vote — that also explains why the Attorney-General can address courts and Parliament alike without being an elected or judicial officeholder.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read together with Article 75(5) (a non-member may serve as Minister for up to six months) — Article 88 is what allows such a Minister (or any Minister sitting in the 'other' House) to actually participate meaningfully in both Houses' proceedings during that period, distinct from and without needing to establish formal membership.

sections.title: The Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Council of States
sections.raw_text:
89. The Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Council of States.—(1) The Vice-President of India shall be ex officio Chairman of the Council of States.
(2) The Council of States shall, as soon as may be, choose a member of the Council to be Deputy Chairman thereof and, so often as the office of Deputy Chairman becomes vacant, the Council shall choose another member to be Deputy Chairman thereof.
key_terms: Deputy Chairman of the Council of States

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 89 confirms and cross-references the Article 64 rule that the Vice-President is automatically (ex officio) the Rajya Sabha's Chairman, and separately requires the Council itself to elect one of its own members as Deputy Chairman — a genuinely elected internal office, unlike the Chairmanship which comes attached to the Vice-Presidency rather than being separately chosen by the House.
essential_elements: Clause (1): the Vice-President is ex officio Chairman of the Council of States (restating Article 64).
Clause (2): the Council of States elects one of its own members as Deputy Chairman, and re-elects a replacement whenever that office falls vacant.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Unlike the Chairman (who holds the post only because of being Vice-President, and vacates it automatically on ceasing to be Vice-President), the Deputy Chairman is directly and separately elected by the House and holds office independent of any other constitutional post.
The Deputy Chairman's own tenure, removal, and resignation are governed by the following Article 90, not by this article.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read together with Article 64 (source of the ex officio Chairmanship) and Articles 90-92 (Deputy Chairman's tenure/removal and presiding restrictions) as one connected unit on Rajya Sabha's presiding officers.

sections.title: Vacation and resignation of, and removal from, the office of Deputy Chairman
sections.raw_text:
90. Vacation and resignation of, and removal from, the office of Deputy Chairman.—A member holding office as Deputy Chairman of the Council of States—
(a) shall vacate his office if he ceases to be a member of the Council;
(b) may at any time, by writing under his hand addressed to the Chairman, resign his office; and
(c) may be removed from his office by a resolution of the Council passed by a majority of all the then members of the Council:
Provided that no resolution for the purpose of clause (c) shall be moved unless at least fourteen days' notice has been given of the intention to move the resolution.
key_terms: automatic vacation of Deputy Chairman office
removal of Deputy Chairman by Council resolution

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 90 governs how a Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha leaves office: automatically on ceasing to be a Council member at all, voluntarily by written resignation addressed to the Chairman, or involuntarily by a simple-majority resolution of the full Council's then-membership, provided at least fourteen days' notice of the removal motion is given in advance.
essential_elements: Clause (a): automatic vacation if the person stops being a member of the Council of States for any reason (e.g., term expiry, resignation from membership).

Clause (b): voluntary resignation by writing under the Deputy Chairman's own hand, addressed to the Chairman (not the President, contrast with the Chairman/Vice-President's own resignation channel under Article 67(a) which goes to the President).

Clause (c) and its proviso: removal by an ordinary majority resolution of all then members of the Council (not two-thirds), but only after at least fourteen days' advance notice of intent to move the resolution.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Removal under clause (c) requires only a simple majority of the Council's total then-membership — a materially lower threshold than the two-thirds supermajority required to remove the Vice-President (who is the ex officio Chairman) under Article 67(b).
The fourteen-day notice proviso is a mandatory procedural precondition; a removal resolution moved without it is not validly before the House.
breakdown.how_to_read: Contrast the simple-majority removal threshold here against the higher supermajority thresholds elsewhere (two-thirds for Presidential impeachment under Article 61, majority-of-all-members-plus-Lok-Sabha-concurrence for Vice-Presidential removal under Article 67(b)) — internal presiding-officer removals are generally easier to effect than removal of the principal constitutional office-holders themselves.

sections.title: Power of the Deputy Chairman or other person to perform the duties of the office of, or to act as, Chairman
sections.raw_text:
91. Power of the Deputy Chairman or other person to perform the duties of the office of, or to act as, Chairman.—(1) While the office of Chairman is vacant, or during any period when the Vice-President is acting as, or discharging the functions of, President, the duties of the office shall be performed by the Deputy Chairman, or, if the office of Deputy Chairman is also vacant, by such member of the Council of States as the President may appoint for the purpose.
(2) During the absence of the Chairman from any sitting of the Council of States the Deputy Chairman, or, if he is also absent, such person as may be determined by the rules of procedure of the Council, or, if no such person is present, such other person as may be determined by the Council, shall act as Chairman.
key_terms: Deputy Chairman performing Chairman's duties during vacancy

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 91 provides the fallback chain ensuring the Rajya Sabha always has someone presiding: if the Chairmanship itself is vacant (or the Vice-President is temporarily consumed with acting as/discharging President's functions under Article 65), the Deputy Chairman steps in, with a further fallback to a President-appointed member if the Deputy Chairmanship is also vacant; separately, for mere day-to-day absence from a particular sitting (not a structural vacancy), the Deputy Chairman or a rules-determined substitute presides instead.
essential_elements: Clause (1): covers structural gaps — an actual vacancy in the Chairmanship, or the Vice-President being occupied acting as/discharging the President's functions — triggering the Deputy Chairman (or, if that office is also vacant, a Council member the President appoints) to perform the Chairman's duties.

Clause (2): covers mere temporary absence from a specific sitting (Chairmanship not vacant, Vice-President not otherwise occupied) — the Deputy Chairman acts, with further fallbacks to a person under the Council's own procedural rules, or a person the Council itself determines.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (1)'s trigger for a 'vacancy' expressly includes the scenario where the Vice-President is acting as, or discharging the functions of, President under Article 65 — even though the Vice-President hasn't technically vacated the Vice-Presidency, their Rajya Sabha Chairmanship function is treated as vacant for this purpose (consistent with the Article 64 proviso).

The two clauses address genuinely different situations (structural vacancy/incapacity vs. one-off absence from a sitting) and use different fallback chains — clause (1)'s ultimate fallback is a Presidential appointment, while clause (2)'s ultimate fallback is the Council's own determination.
breakdown.how_to_read: Cross-reference Article 64's proviso (which already flags that the Chairmanship function is suspended during an Article 65 acting-Presidency) and Article 92 (which separately bars the Chairman/Deputy Chairman from presiding over their own removal resolution, applying clause (2)'s absence-substitute mechanism by extension).

sections.title: The Chairman or the Deputy Chairman not to preside while a resolution for his removal from office is under consideration
sections.raw_text:
92. The Chairman or the Deputy Chairman not to preside while a resolution for his removal from office is under consideration.—(1) At any sitting of the Council of States, while any resolution for the removal of the Vice-President from his office is under consideration, the Chairman, or while any resolution for the removal of the Deputy Chairman from his office is under consideration, the Deputy Chairman, shall not, though he is present, preside, and the provisions of clause (2) of article 91 shall apply in relation to every such sitting as they apply in relation to a sitting from which the Chairman, or, as the case may be, the Deputy Chairman, is absent.
(2) The Chairman shall have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, the Council of States while any resolution for the removal of the Vice-President from his office is under consideration in the Council, but, notwithstanding anything in article 100, shall not be entitled to vote at all on such resolution or on any other matter during such proceedings.
key_terms: no presiding over own removal resolution
Chairman's speaking right without voting during own removal debate

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 92 applies a basic natural-justice principle to the Rajya Sabha's own presiding officers: neither the Chairman (i.e., the Vice-President, whose removal is governed by Article 67(b)) nor the Deputy Chairman may preside over a sitting while a resolution to remove them is under consideration — even though physically present, the Article 91(2) absence-substitute mechanism takes over — and, specifically for the Chairman, clause (2) permits participation in debate on their own removal but expressly bars any vote at all on that resolution or anything else during those proceedings.
essential_elements: Clause (1): bars the Chairman from presiding during consideration of a Vice-Presidential removal resolution, and bars the Deputy Chairman from presiding during consideration of a Deputy Chairman removal resolution, treating the sitting as if that officer were absent (triggering Article 91(2)'s substitute-presiding mechanism).

Clause (2): specifically for the Chairman, grants a right to speak and otherwise participate in the debate on his own removal resolution, but completely denies any voting right — on that resolution or on any other matter — during the entire course of those proceedings, overriding the general voting rule in Article 100.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (2)'s total voting bar (even on unrelated matters arising during the same proceedings) is broader than a simple recusal from the removal vote alone — it suspends the Chairman's vote entirely for the duration of the removal-resolution proceedings.

The article textually addresses the Chairman's total voting bar in clause (2) but is silent on an equivalent express provision for the Deputy Chairman's voting rights during his own removal proceedings — Article 96(2) (the House of the People's parallel provision for the Speaker) instead grants a limited casting-vote-only right, illustrating that the analogous Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha provisions are not perfectly symmetric.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read as the natural-justice safeguard completing the Article 89-91 sequence on Rajya Sabha presiding officers — compare directly against Articles 95-96 (the mirror-image provisions for the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha) to see how the two Houses' internal removal-safeguard mechanics differ slightly in their voting-right specifics.

sections.title: The Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of the People
sections.raw_text: 93. The Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of the People.—The House of the People shall, as soon as may be, choose two members of the House to be respectively Speaker and Deputy Speaker thereof and, so often as the office of Speaker or Deputy Speaker becomes vacant, the House shall choose another member to be Speaker or Deputy Speaker, as the case may be.
key_terms: Speaker of the House of the People
Deputy Speaker of the House of the People

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 93 requires the Lok Sabha to elect its own Speaker and Deputy Speaker from among its members — unlike the Rajya Sabha's Chairman, who is not separately elected by the House but comes attached to the Vice-Presidency, both Lok Sabha presiding offices are directly chosen by the House itself, and refilled by fresh election whenever either falls vacant.
essential_elements: The House of the People must choose two of its own members to be Speaker and Deputy Speaker respectively, as soon as practicable after being constituted.
Whenever either office falls vacant, the House must again choose another member to fill it.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Unlike the Rajya Sabha's Chairman (an ex officio position tied to the Vice-Presidency), both the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha are genuinely, directly elected by and from the House's own membership — there is no equivalent ex officio arrangement in the Lok Sabha.

The proviso to Article 94(c) (continuity of the Speaker despite dissolution) means the Speaker's office does not actually fall vacant simply because the House is dissolved, softening the practical frequency of re-election under this article.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read together with Articles 94-96 (vacation/resignation/removal, acting arrangements, and the no-presiding-over-own-removal rule) as the Lok Sabha's mirror sequence to Articles 89-92 for the Rajya Sabha — note the structural difference that the Lok Sabha has no ex officio equivalent to the Vice-President-as-Chairman arrangement.

sections.title: Vacation and resignation of, and removal from, the offices of Speaker and Deputy Speaker
sections.raw_text:
94. Vacation and resignation of, and removal from, the offices of Speaker and Deputy Speaker.—A member holding office as Speaker or Deputy Speaker of the House of the People—
(a) shall vacate his office if he ceases to be a member of the House of the People;
(b) may at any time, by writing under his hand addressed, if such member is the Speaker, to the Deputy Speaker, and if such member is the Deputy Speaker, to the Speaker, resign his office; and
(c) may be removed from his office by a resolution of the House of the People passed by a majority of all the then members of the House:
Provided that no resolution for the purpose of clause (c) shall be moved unless at least fourteen days' notice has been given of the intention to move the resolution:
Provided further that, whenever the House of the People is dissolved, the Speaker shall not vacate his office until immediately before the first meeting of the House of the People after the dissolution.
key_terms: automatic vacation of Speaker/Deputy Speaker office
resignation of Speaker to Deputy Speaker and vice versa
removal of Speaker by House resolution

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 94 mirrors Article 90's Rajya Sabha scheme for the Lok Sabha's Speaker and Deputy Speaker — automatic vacation on ceasing to be a House member, resignation addressed cross-wise (Speaker to Deputy Speaker, Deputy Speaker to Speaker), and removal by a simple-majority resolution of the full House with fourteen days' advance notice — but adds a crucial second proviso unique to the Lok Sabha: because the House itself is periodically dissolved (unlike the permanent Rajya Sabha), the Speaker specifically continues in office right up until immediately before the newly constituted House's first meeting, ensuring there is never a leaderless gap during dissolution and fresh elections.
essential_elements: Clause (a): automatic vacation on ceasing to be a member of the House of the People.
Clause (b): resignation by writing under the office-holder's own hand — Speaker resigns to the Deputy Speaker, Deputy Speaker resigns to the Speaker.
Clause (c) and its first proviso: removal by simple-majority resolution of all then members of the House, only after at least fourteen days' advance notice.

Second proviso: despite House dissolution (which would otherwise trigger clause (a), since dissolution ends everyone's membership), the Speaker specifically continues in office until immediately before the newly elected House's first meeting.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The second proviso's continuity protection applies only to the Speaker, not the Deputy Speaker — a Deputy Speaker's office does end on dissolution in the ordinary course under clause (a), requiring a fresh Deputy Speaker election once the new House is constituted.

This continuity rule exists precisely because dissolution is a recurring, expected event for the Lok Sabha (unlike the never-dissolved Rajya Sabha), so Article 94 had to build in an express carve-out that Article 90 (for the permanent Rajya Sabha) never needed.
breakdown.how_to_read: The second proviso is the key textual difference from Article 90 — flag it whenever comparing the two provisions, since it directly follows from the structural difference between the dissolvable Lok Sabha (Article 83(2)) and the permanent Rajya Sabha (Article 83(1)).

sections.title: Power of the Deputy Speaker or other person to perform the duties of the office of, or to act as, Speaker
sections.raw_text:
95. Power of the Deputy Speaker or other person to perform the duties of the office of, or to act as, Speaker.—(1) While the office of Speaker is vacant, the duties of the office shall be performed by the Deputy Speaker or, if the office of Deputy Speaker is also vacant, by such member of the House of the People as the President may appoint for the purpose.
(2) During the absence of the Speaker from any sitting of the House of the People the Deputy Speaker or, if he is also absent, such person as may be determined by the rules of procedure of the House, or, if no such person is present, such other person as may be determined by the House, shall act as Speaker.
key_terms: Deputy Speaker performing Speaker's duties during vacancy

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 95 mirrors Article 91's Rajya Sabha fallback structure for the Lok Sabha: a vacancy in the Speaker's office is filled by the Deputy Speaker, or (if that office is also vacant) by a President-appointed House member, while mere absence from a particular sitting is covered by the Deputy Speaker or a rules-determined/House-determined substitute — the same two-tier vacancy-versus-absence distinction as Article 91, without the Article 65 acting-Presidency trigger that has no Lok Sabha equivalent.
essential_elements: Clause (1): a structural vacancy in the Speaker's office is filled by the Deputy Speaker, with a further fallback to a President-appointed member of the House if the Deputy Speakership is also vacant.

Clause (2): mere absence of the Speaker from a specific sitting is covered by the Deputy Speaker, or, if also absent, a person determined under the House's own procedural rules, or, failing that, a person the House itself determines.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Unlike Article 91(1)'s Rajya Sabha version, Article 95(1) has no equivalent 'Vice-President acting as President' trigger — because the Lok Sabha's Speaker has no ex officio linkage to any other constitutional office the way the Rajya Sabha's Chairman does to the Vice-Presidency.

As with Article 91, the vacancy-fallback chain (clause 1) and absence-fallback chain (clause 2) are structurally parallel but distinct, with different ultimate fallback appointers (President vs. the House itself).
breakdown.how_to_read: Read as the direct structural mirror of Article 91, minus the acting-Presidency trigger — useful for spotting exactly how the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha presiding-officer-substitution schemes diverge only where the underlying office (Chairman tied to Vice-Presidency vs. Speaker standalone) differs.

sections.title: The Speaker or the Deputy Speaker not to preside while a resolution for his removal from office is under consideration
sections.raw_text:
96. The Speaker or the Deputy Speaker not to preside while a resolution for his removal from office is under consideration.—(1) At any sitting of the House of the People, while any resolution for the removal of the Speaker from his office is under consideration, the Speaker, or while any resolution for the removal of the Deputy Speaker from his office is under consideration, the Deputy Speaker, shall not, though he is present, preside, and the provisions of clause (2) of article 95 shall apply in relation to every such sitting as they apply in relation to a sitting from which the Speaker, or, as the case may be, the Deputy Speaker, is absent.
(2) The Speaker shall have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, the House of the People while any resolution for his removal from office is under consideration in the House and shall, notwithstanding anything in article 100, be entitled to vote only in the first instance on such resolution or on any other matter during such proceedings but not in the case of an equality of votes.
key_terms: no presiding over own removal resolution (Speaker)
Speaker's limited voting right during own removal debate

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 96 is the Lok Sabha's mirror of Article 92, with one notable textual difference in the voting-rights detail: the Speaker cannot preside during consideration of their own removal resolution (Article 95(2)'s absence-substitute mechanism applies instead), and while the Speaker retains a right to speak and participate in that debate, their voting right is narrower than an ordinary member's but not zero — they may vote only in the first instance (as an ordinary voter would, on any matter arising during those proceedings) but specifically lose the casting vote they would otherwise exercise under Article 100 in case of a tie.
essential_elements: Clause (1): bars the Speaker from presiding while a resolution for the Speaker's own removal is under consideration, and bars the Deputy Speaker from presiding while a resolution for the Deputy Speaker's own removal is under consideration, triggering Article 95(2)'s substitute-presiding mechanism as if absent.

Clause (2): the Speaker may speak and participate in the debate on their own removal, and may vote in the first instance on that resolution or any other matter during the proceedings, but is denied the casting vote in case of a tie that Article 100 would otherwise give the presiding officer.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This differs from Article 92(2)'s treatment of the Rajya Sabha Chairman, who is denied any vote at all during removal proceedings — Article 96(2) instead gives the Speaker an ordinary first-instance vote but strips only the tie-breaking casting vote, a materially less restrictive rule.

The provision applies specifically to the Speaker's own removal; the article does not spell out an equivalent express voting entitlement for the Deputy Speaker during a resolution for the Deputy Speaker's own removal, paralleling the same asymmetry noted under Article 92.
breakdown.how_to_read: Directly contrast clause (2) against Article 92(2) (total voting ban for the Rajya Sabha Chairman during his own removal) — this is a frequently tested textual distinction between the two Houses' otherwise parallel presiding-officer-removal safeguards.

sections.title: Salaries and allowances of the Chairman and Deputy Chairman and the Speaker and Deputy Speaker
sections.raw_text: 97. Salaries and allowances of the Chairman and Deputy Chairman and the Speaker and Deputy Speaker.—There shall be paid to the Chairman and the Deputy Chairman of the Council of States, and to the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the House of the People, such salaries and allowances as may be respectively fixed by Parliament by law and, until provision in that behalf is so made, such salaries and allowances as are specified in the Second Schedule.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 97 fixes how the four Parliamentary presiding officers — Rajya Sabha's Chairman and Deputy Chairman, Lok Sabha's Speaker and Deputy Speaker — are paid: Parliament sets their salaries and allowances by ordinary law, defaulting to the Second Schedule's specified rates until Parliament actually legislates on the point, exactly the same default-to-Second-Schedule pattern used for Ministers under Article 75(6).
essential_elements: Covers four offices: Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Council of States, and Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of the People.
Salaries/allowances are fixed by Parliament through ordinary law.
In the absence of such a law, the Second Schedule's specified rates apply by default.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a straightforward machinery provision with the same 'law, defaulting to Second Schedule' structure seen repeatedly elsewhere (Ministers under Article 75(6), and later the President's and Governors' emoluments provisions) — the substantive amounts themselves live in the Second Schedule or in Parliamentary legislation, not in the article's own text.
breakdown.how_to_read: Recognise the recurring 'Parliament may fix by law, until then the Second Schedule governs' template — it appears for Ministers (Article 75(6)) and here for the four presiding officers, and will recur for other constitutional office-holders' emoluments later in the document.

sections.title: Secretariat of Parliament
sections.raw_text:
98. Secretariat of Parliament.—(1) Each House of Parliament shall have a separate secretarial staff:
Provided that nothing in this clause shall be construed as preventing the creation of posts common to both Houses of Parliament.
(2) Parliament may by law regulate the recruitment, and the conditions of service of persons appointed, to the secretarial staff of either House of Parliament.
(3) Until provision is made by Parliament under clause (2), the President may, after consultation with the Speaker of the House of the People or the Chairman of the Council of States, as the case may be, make rules regulating the recruitment, and the conditions of service of persons appointed, to the secretarial staff of either House of Parliament, and any rules so made shall have effect subject to the provisions of any law made under the said clause.
key_terms: separate secretarial staff for each House
common posts between the two Houses
Parliament's law-making power over secretariat service conditions
President's interim rule-making power for secretariat (Article 98(3))

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 98 gives each House of Parliament its own administrative secretariat, distinct from the executive branch's civil service — protecting Parliament's institutional independence from the Government of the day — while allowing common posts shared between both Houses where efficient, and vesting recruitment/service-condition rule-making primarily in Parliament by law, with the President (after consulting the relevant presiding officer) empowered to make interim rules until Parliament legislates.
essential_elements: Clause (1) main text: each House has its own separate secretarial staff.
Proviso to clause (1): common posts serving both Houses may still be created, despite the general separateness rule.
Clause (2): Parliament may by law regulate recruitment and service conditions for either House's secretarial staff.

Clause (3): until Parliament legislates under clause (2), the President — after consulting the Speaker (for Lok Sabha staff) or the Chairman (for Rajya Sabha staff) — may make interim rules on the same subject, which remain subject to being overridden by any law Parliament later makes.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The proviso to clause (1) is itself an exception to the 'separate staff' default, permitting shared/common posts for administrative efficiency without undermining each House's institutional autonomy for the bulk of its staffing.

Clause (3)'s Presidential rule-making is expressly interim and subordinate — any rules made under it operate 'subject to the provisions of any law made under' clause (2), meaning Parliament's legislation always prevails once enacted.
breakdown.how_to_read: This closes out the 'Officers of Parliament' sub-heading (Articles 89-98) before the 'Conduct of Business' sub-heading begins at Article 99 — read it as the administrative-independence counterpart to the presiding-officer provisions just covered, ensuring Parliament controls its own staff rather than depending on the executive.

sections.title: Oath or affirmation by members
sections.raw_text: 99. Oath or affirmation by members.—Every member of either House of Parliament shall, before taking his seat, make and subscribe before the President, or some person appointed in that behalf by him, an oath or affirmation according to the form set out for the purpose in the Third Schedule.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 99 requires every elected or nominated Member of Parliament to make and subscribe the prescribed Third Schedule oath or affirmation before the President (or a President-appointed person) before actually taking their seat — this is the post-election formality, distinct from the pre-candidacy oath under Article 84(a), and Article 104 backs it with a financial penalty for anyone who sits or votes without having complied.
essential_elements: Applies to every member of either House, whether elected or nominated.
The oath/affirmation must be made and subscribed before the President or a person the President appoints for that purpose.
It must occur before the member takes their seat, and uses the specific form prescribed in the Third Schedule.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is distinct from the Article 84(a) oath, which is a pre-candidacy prerequisite taken before an Election Commission-authorised person; Article 99's oath is taken after election, before actually sitting as a member.
Failure to comply before sitting or voting triggers the Article 104 monetary penalty, making this a substantively enforced formality rather than a purely ceremonial one.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read directly alongside Article 104 (the penalty for sitting/voting without complying) and Article 84(a) (the earlier, pre-candidacy oath) to see the full oath-taking lifecycle of a Member of Parliament.

sections.title: Voting in Houses, power of Houses to act notwithstanding vacancies and quorum
sections.raw_text:
100. Voting in Houses, power of Houses to act notwithstanding vacancies and quorum.—(1) Save as otherwise provided in this Constitution, all questions at any sitting of either House or joint sitting of the Houses shall be determined by a majority of votes of the members present and voting, other than the Speaker or person acting as Chairman or Speaker.
The Chairman or Speaker, or person acting as such, shall not vote in the first instance, but shall have and exercise a casting vote in the case of an equality of votes.
(2) Either House of Parliament shall have power to act notwithstanding any vacancy in the membership thereof, and any proceedings in Parliament shall be valid notwithstanding that it is discovered subsequently that some person who was not entitled so to do sat or voted or otherwise took part in the proceedings.
(3) Until Parliament by law otherwise provides, the quorum to constitute a meeting of either House of Parliament shall be one-tenth of the total number of members of the House.
(4) If at any time during a meeting of a House there is no quorum, it shall be the duty of the Chairman or Speaker, or person acting as such, either to adjourn the House or to suspend the meeting until there is a quorum.
key_terms: majority of members present and voting

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 100 lays down the ordinary mechanics of how Parliament actually transacts business: decisions are made by majority of members present and voting (the presiding officer abstaining in the first instance but breaking ties with a casting vote), a House can validly function despite vacant seats, proceedings remain valid even if it later emerges someone who sat or voted wasn't actually entitled to, and — until Parliament legislates otherwise — a quorum of just one-tenth of a House's total membership is enough to hold a valid sitting, with the presiding officer required to adjourn or suspend the sitting if quorum is lost.
essential_elements: Clause (1): ordinary questions are decided by majority of members present and voting; the presiding officer doesn't vote in the first instance but casts the deciding vote on a tie.
Clause (2): a House may validly act despite vacancies in its membership, and proceedings are not invalidated merely because it later emerges an ineligible person participated.
Clause (3): the default quorum (absent a Parliamentary law fixing a different figure) is one-tenth of the House's total membership.
Clause (4): if quorum is lost during a sitting, the presiding officer must either adjourn the House or suspend the meeting until quorum is restored.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (1)'s general majority-vote rule yields to the Constitution's own specific exceptions ('save as otherwise provided') — e.g., the supermajority thresholds for a Presidential/Vice-Presidential impeachment resolution (Articles 61, 67(b)) or a constitutional amendment (Article 368).

Clause (1)'s casting-vote rule for the presiding officer is itself modified for the Rajya Sabha Chairman during his own removal proceedings (Article 92(2), zero vote at all) and for the Lok Sabha Speaker during his own removal proceedings (Article 96(2), first-instance vote but no casting vote) — this Article 100 rule is the default that those two provisions carve exceptions from.
The one-tenth quorum figure in clause (3) is itself only a default, alterable by Parliament through ordinary law.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this as the default procedural engine of Parliament — always check first whether the Constitution supplies a specific supermajority or special voting rule elsewhere before applying Article 100's general majority/quorum defaults.

sections.title: Vacation of seats
sections.raw_text:
101. Vacation of seats.—(1) No person shall be a member of both Houses of Parliament and provision shall be made by Parliament by law for the vacation by a person who is chosen a member of both Houses of his seat in one House or the other.
(2) No person shall be a member both of Parliament and of a House of the Legislature of a State, and if a person is chosen a member both of Parliament and of a House of the Legislature of a State, then, at the expiration of such period as may be specified in rules made by the President, that person's seat in Parliament shall become vacant, unless he has previously resigned his seat in the Legislature of the State.
(3) If a member of either House of Parliament—
(a) becomes subject to any of the disqualifications mentioned in clause (1) or clause (2) of article 102, or
(b) resigns his seat by writing under his hand addressed to the Chairman or the Speaker, as the case may be, and his resignation is accepted by the Chairman or the Speaker, as the case may be,
his seat shall thereupon become vacant:
Provided that in the case of any resignation referred to in sub-clause (b), if from information received or otherwise and after making such inquiry as he thinks fit, the Chairman or the Speaker, as the case may be, is satisfied that such resignation is not voluntary or genuine, he shall not accept such resignation.
(4) If for a period of sixty days a member of either House of Parliament is without permission of the House absent from all meetings thereof, the House may declare his seat vacant:
Provided that in computing the said period of sixty days no account shall be taken of any period during which the House is prorogued or is adjourned for more than four consecutive days.
key_terms: no simultaneous membership of both Houses
no simultaneous membership of Parliament and State Legislature
presiding officer's inquiry into genuineness of resignation

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 101 lists the ways a Parliamentary seat becomes vacant: structurally, no one may sit in both Houses of Parliament at once, or in Parliament and a State Legislature at once (a grace period lets the person choose which to keep); individually, a seat vacates automatically on incurring an Article 102 disqualification or on a resignation the presiding officer accepts as genuinely voluntary (a 1974 amendment specifically empowering the Chairman/Speaker to refuse a resignation they find involuntary or not genuine, closing a loophole against coerced or backdated resignations); and a House may itself declare a seat vacant if a member is absent from all sittings for sixty days without permission (with prorogation/long adjournment periods excluded from that count).
essential_elements: Clause (1): dual membership of both Houses of Parliament simultaneously is barred; Parliament must legislate the mechanics for the person to vacate one seat.
Clause (2): dual membership of Parliament and a State Legislature is barred; the Parliamentary seat becomes vacant after a President-fixed grace period unless the person resigns the State seat first.
Clause (3)(a): seat vacates automatically on becoming subject to an Article 102(1) or (2) disqualification.

Clause (3)(b) and its proviso: seat vacates on a written resignation to the Chairman/Speaker, but only once the presiding officer accepts it — and the presiding officer must refuse acceptance if, after appropriate inquiry, they are satisfied the resignation isn't voluntary or genuine.

Clause (4) and its proviso: sixty consecutive days of unauthorised total absence lets the House declare the seat vacant, with prorogation periods and adjournments exceeding four consecutive days excluded from the sixty-day count.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The resignation-acceptance safeguard in the proviso to clause (3)(b) was inserted by the 33rd Amendment (1974) specifically to prevent pressured or coerced resignations from taking automatic effect — before that amendment, a tendered resignation took effect without any discretionary check.
Clause (4)'s sixty-day count deliberately excludes prorogation periods and long adjournments, so a member is not penalised for absence during periods when the House itself wasn't functioning.

Clause (2)'s grace period (fixed by Presidential rules, not the article itself) gives a dual-elected person a window to choose and resign from one body before automatic vacation kicks in — it is not an indefinite dual-membership allowance.
