breakdown.how_to_read: Read clause (3)(a) together with Article 102 (the disqualification grounds it cross-references) and treat the clause (3)(b) proviso as a landmark post-1974 safeguard worth flagging whenever discussing 'resignation acceptance' as a discretionary, not ministerial, act of the presiding officer.

sections.title: Disqualifications for membership

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 102 lists the grounds disqualifying a person from being chosen as, or continuing to be, a Member of Parliament: holding a non-exempted office of profit under the Union or a State, being adjudged of unsound mind by a competent court, being an undischarged insolvent, lacking Indian citizenship or holding foreign citizenship/allegiance, or being disqualified by any Parliamentary law — plus, since the 52nd Amendment (1985), disqualification under the Tenth Schedule's anti-defection rules, with the Explanation carving Ministers out of the office-of-profit bar since a Minister's office is itself constitutionally contemplated.
essential_elements: Clause (1)(a): office-of-profit disqualification under the Union or any State Government, unless Parliament has declared that particular office exempt by law.
Clause (1)(b): unsoundness of mind, as declared by a competent court.
Clause (1)(c): undischarged insolvency.
Clause (1)(d): not being an Indian citizen, or having voluntarily acquired foreign citizenship, or being under any acknowledgment of allegiance/adherence to a foreign State.
Clause (1)(e): any further disqualification Parliament prescribes by law.
Explanation to clause (1): being a Union or State Minister does not, by itself, count as holding a disqualifying office of profit.
Clause (2) (inserted by the 52nd Amendment, 1985): disqualification under the Tenth Schedule (the anti-defection law) is a freestanding, separate ground.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The office-of-profit bar in clause (1)(a) is not absolute — Parliament can and does exempt specific offices by law, a frequently exercised power (e.g., via the Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act) to allow MPs to hold certain offices (such as parliamentary committee chairs) without disqualification.

The Explanation's carve-out for Ministers exists precisely because Ministers necessarily hold a Union/State government office by design (Articles 74-75) — without this Explanation, every Minister who is also an MP would otherwise be automatically disqualified.

Clause (2)'s Tenth Schedule disqualification operates independently of clause (1) — a member can be disqualified for defection-related reasons even without triggering any of the five clause (1) grounds.
breakdown.how_to_read: Cross-reference the Tenth Schedule directly for the substantive anti-defection rules that clause (2) merely points to, and connect clause (1)(a)'s office-of-profit ground to Article 58(2)/Article 66(4) (the parallel office-of-profit disqualifications for the President and Vice-President) to see the same underlying policy — separating legislative/electoral office from executive patronage — applied at different constitutional levels.

sections.title: Decision on questions as to disqualifications of members
sections.raw_text:
103. Decision on questions as to disqualifications of members.—(1) If any question arises as to whether a member of either House of Parliament has become subject to any of the disqualifications mentioned in clause (1) of article 102, the question shall be referred for the decision of the President and his decision shall be final.
(2) Before giving any decision on any such question, the President shall obtain the opinion of the Election Commission and shall act according to such opinion.
key_terms: President's decision on Article 102(1) disqualification questions

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 103 fixes who resolves a live dispute about whether a sitting MP has become disqualified under one of Article 102(1)'s five grounds: the President decides, and that decision is final — but the President's discretion here is not real discretion at all, since clause (2) mandates first obtaining the Election Commission's opinion and then acting strictly according to that opinion, making the Election Commission the substantive decision-maker in practice while the President supplies only the formal order.
essential_elements: Clause (1): any question of whether a sitting MP has incurred an Article 102(1) disqualification is referred to the President, whose decision is final.

Clause (2): before deciding, the President must obtain the Election Commission's opinion and must act according to that opinion — removing independent Presidential discretion from the substance of the decision.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This article's procedure applies specifically to Article 102(1) disqualifications; questions of disqualification under the Tenth Schedule (Article 102(2), anti-defection) are instead decided by the Speaker or Chairman under the Tenth Schedule's own separate procedure, not through this Article 103 route.

Although called the 'President's decision,' the binding requirement to act according to the Election Commission's opinion means the real adjudicatory function is performed by the Election Commission, with the President's order being a formal implementation of that opinion.
breakdown.how_to_read: Contrast this Article 102(1)-disqualification procedure (President bound by Election Commission opinion) against the separate Tenth Schedule anti-defection procedure (decided by the Speaker/Chairman, subject to judicial review) — a frequently tested distinction on which body decides which category of disqualification.

sections.title: Penalty for sitting and voting before making oath or affirmation under article 99 or when not qualified or when disqualified
sections.raw_text: 104. Penalty for sitting and voting before making oath or affirmation under article 99 or when not qualified or when disqualified.—If a person sits or votes as a member of either House of Parliament before he has complied with the requirements of article 99, or when he knows that he is not qualified or that he is disqualified for membership thereof, or that he is prohibited from so doing by the provisions of any law made by Parliament, he shall be liable in respect of each day on which he so sits or votes to a penalty of five hundred rupees to be recovered as a debt due to the Union.
key_terms: penalty for sitting/voting without oath or while disqualified

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 104 backs Article 99's oath requirement and Article 102's disqualification rules with a per-day monetary penalty (five hundred rupees for each day of violation) for anyone who sits or votes in either House before taking the required oath, or while knowingly unqualified, disqualified, or otherwise legally prohibited from sitting — the penalty being recoverable as an ordinary debt owed to the Union.
essential_elements: Applies to a person who sits or votes as an MP without having complied with the Article 99 oath requirement.
Also applies to a person who sits or votes while knowing they are not qualified, are disqualified, or are otherwise prohibited by Parliamentary law from doing so.
Penalty: five hundred rupees for each day the violation continues, recoverable as a debt due to the Union.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The knowledge requirement ('when he knows') for the not-qualified/disqualified/prohibited limbs means the penalty targets knowing violations in those categories, whereas the oath-noncompliance limb applies regardless of the person's state of knowledge.

This is a fixed statutory penalty figure written directly into the constitutional text (unlike many other financial provisions that defer to Parliamentary law or the Second Schedule) and has not been revised for inflation since 1950.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read as the enforcement backstop for Articles 99 and 102 — without this penalty provision, the oath and disqualification requirements would lack any explicit sanction for a member who simply ignores them and continues sitting/voting.

sections.title: Powers, privileges, etc., of the Houses of Parliament and of the members and committees thereof
sections.raw_text:
105. Powers, privileges, etc., of the Houses of Parliament and of the members and committees thereof.—(1) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution and to the rules and standing orders regulating the procedure of Parliament, there shall be freedom of speech in Parliament.
(2) No member of Parliament shall be liable to any proceedings in any court in respect of anything said or any vote given by him in Parliament or any committee thereof, and no person shall be so liable in respect of the publication by or under the authority of either House of Parliament of any report, paper, votes or proceedings.
(3) In other respects, the powers, privileges and immunities of each House of Parliament, and of the members and the committees of each House, shall be such as may from time to time be defined by Parliament by law, and, until so defined, shall be those of that House and of its members and committees immediately before the coming into force of section 15 of the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978.
(4) The provisions of clauses (1), (2) and (3) shall apply in relation to persons who by virtue of this Constitution have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, a House of Parliament or any committee thereof as they apply in relation to members of Parliament.
key_terms: immunity from court proceedings for parliamentary speech/vote
immunity for authorised publication of proceedings
residual powers privileges and immunities of Parliament
extension of privileges to non-member participants

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 105 is the parliamentary-privilege provision protecting Parliament's ability to debate and function without fear of external (especially judicial) interference: it guarantees freedom of speech within Parliament (subject to the House's own procedural rules), immunises members from court proceedings over anything said or any vote cast in Parliament or its committees, extends the same immunity to authorised publication of Parliament's own reports/papers/proceedings, and leaves all other powers/privileges/immunities to be defined by Parliament itself by law (defaulting, until such a law is made, to whatever privileges existed immediately before the 44th Amendment took effect in 1979) — with clause (4) extending all of this to non-member participants like Ministers and the Attorney-General who have a right to speak under Article 88.
essential_elements: Clause (1): freedom of speech in Parliament, subject to the Constitution and Parliament's own rules/standing orders.

Clause (2): absolute immunity from court proceedings for anything said or any vote given in Parliament or a committee, and equivalent immunity for authorised publication of Parliamentary reports/papers/proceedings.
Clause (3): all other powers, privileges, and immunities are as Parliament defines by law from time to time, defaulting to the pre-44th-Amendment (pre-1979) position until such a law is made.

Clause (4): extends clauses (1)-(3) to any person who has a constitutional right to speak/participate in a House or committee without being a member — chiefly Ministers and the Attorney-General under Article 88.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The clause (2) immunity is specifically for 'anything said or any vote given' in Parliament/committee proceedings — it does not immunise conduct unrelated to speech or voting within the House, nor conduct outside Parliament's proceedings altogether.

Clause (1)'s freedom of speech is itself made 'subject to the provisions of this Constitution' — meaning it does not override other constitutional limits — and 'subject to... the rules and standing orders' of Parliament, meaning the House's own procedure can regulate (though not eliminate) how that freedom is exercised.

Clause (3) leaves an open-ended category of privileges undefined by the Constitution itself, historically borrowing from British House of Commons practice as the pre-1979 default baseline, a point of ongoing debate about the precise scope of 'privilege' in the absence of a comprehensive Parliamentary codification.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the Union-legislature counterpart to Article 194 (identical privilege scheme for State Legislatures) — read them together, and note clause (2)'s absolute immunity is what shields MPs from defamation or other civil/criminal proceedings over their speech or votes strictly within Parliamentary proceedings.

sections.title: Salaries and allowances of members
sections.raw_text: 106. Salaries and allowances of members.—Members of either House of Parliament shall be entitled to receive such salaries and allowances as may from time to time be determined by Parliament by law and, until provision in that respect is so made, allowances at such rates and upon such conditions as were immediately before the commencement of this Constitution applicable in the case of members of the Constituent Assembly of the Dominion of India.
key_terms: salaries and allowances of Members of Parliament

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 106 entitles every MP to salaries and allowances Parliament determines by law from time to time, with a historical default (rather than the usual Second Schedule default) applicable only until Parliament first legislates on the point: the rates and conditions that applied to members of the Constituent Assembly of the Dominion of India immediately before the Constitution commenced.
essential_elements: MPs are entitled to salaries/allowances as Parliament determines by ordinary law.
Absent such a law, the default is the pre-commencement Constituent Assembly of the Dominion of India's rates and conditions — a one-time historical baseline rather than a Schedule-based figure.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is the one salary/allowance provision in this cluster that does not default to the Second Schedule (contrast Article 97 for presiding officers and Article 75(6) for Ministers) — it instead points to a specific pre-constitutional historical baseline, reflecting that this article predates any need for a fresh Schedule-based default since Parliament was expected to legislate promptly.
breakdown.how_to_read: Compare against Article 97's Second-Schedule-default pattern for presiding officers — Article 106 is a slightly different (historical-baseline) default mechanism for ordinary members' pay, useful for spotting the Constitution's varying default-salary techniques across different offices.

sections.title: Provisions as to introduction and passing of Bills
sections.raw_text: (1) Subject to the provisions of articles 109 and 117 with respect to Money Bills and other financial Bills, a Bill may originate in either House of Parliament. (2) Subject to the provisions of articles 108 and 109, a Bill shall not be deemed to have been passed by the Houses of Parliament unless it has been agreed to by both Houses, either without amendment or with such amendments only as are agreed to by both Houses. (3) A Bill pending in Parliament shall not lapse by reason of the prorogation of the Houses. (4) A Bill pending in the Council of States which has not been passed by the House of the People shall not lapse on a dissolution of the House of the People. (5) A Bill which is pending in the House of the People, or which having been passed by the House of the People is pending in the Council of States, shall, subject to the provisions of article 108, lapse on a dissolution of the House of the People.
key_terms: prorogation does not lapse a Bill

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the master rule for how an ordinary Bill moves through Parliament. Article 107(1) lets a Bill start in either House (subject to Money/financial Bill restrictions elsewhere). Article 107(2) says a Bill is only 'passed' once both Houses agree to identical text. Clause (3) protects Bills from being killed by a mere prorogation (session end) — they carry over to the next session. But clauses (4) and (5) draw a sharp line at dissolution (Lok Sabha's five-year term ending or early dissolution): a Bill still sitting in the Lok Sabha, or passed by the Lok Sabha but still pending in the Rajya Sabha, dies — while a Bill introduced in and still pending only in the Rajya Sabha (never sent to or passed by the Lok Sabha) survives dissolution, reflecting the Rajya Sabha's permanent character under Article 83(1).
essential_elements: A Bill may originate in either House, subject to Articles 109 and 117 restricting Money Bills and financial Bills to the Lok Sabha
A Bill counts as 'passed' by Parliament only when both Houses agree to the same text, with or without amendments
Prorogation of either House does not cause a pending Bill to lapse
A Bill pending only in the Rajya Sabha, not yet passed by the Lok Sabha, survives a Lok Sabha dissolution
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (5) is itself subject to Article 108 — if a joint sitting has been validly triggered before dissolution, the Bill can still be revived and passed at that joint sitting under Article 108(5), notwithstanding the general lapsing rule
Money Bills and other financial Bills covered by Articles 109 and 117 are carved out of the general dual-origination rule in clause (1) and can only originate in the House of the People
breakdown.how_to_read: Read clause (2) as the definition of 'passed by Parliament,' and clauses (3)-(5) as the lapsing rules distinguishing prorogation (harmless) from dissolution (fatal, except for Rajya Sabha-only-pending Bills) — this article is the backbone for understanding why some Bills survive elections and others don't.

sections.title: Joint sitting of both Houses in certain cases
sections.raw_text: (1) If after a Bill has been passed by one House and transmitted to the other House— (a) the Bill is rejected by the other House; or (b) the Houses have finally disagreed as to the amendments to be made in the Bill; or (c) more than six months elapse from the date of the reception of the Bill by the other House without the Bill being passed by it, the President may, unless the Bill has elapsed by reason of a dissolution of the House of the People, notify to the Houses by message if they are sitting or by public notification if they are not sitting, his intention to summon them to meet in a joint sitting for the purpose of deliberating and voting on the Bill: Provided that nothing in this clause shall apply to a Money Bill. (2) In reckoning any such period of six months as is referred to in clause (1), no account shall be taken of any period during which the House referred to in sub-clause (c) of that clause is prorogued or adjourned for more than four consecutive days. (3) Where the President has under clause (1) notified his intention of summoning the Houses to meet in a joint sitting, neither House shall proceed further with the Bill, but the President may at any time after the date of his notification summon the Houses to meet in a joint sitting for the purpose specified in the notification and, if he does so, the Houses shall meet accordingly. (4) If at the joint sitting of the two Houses the Bill, with such amendments, if any, as are agreed to in joint sitting, is passed by a majority of the total number of members of both Houses present and voting, it shall be deemed for the purposes of this Constitution to have been passed by both Houses: Provided that at a joint sitting— (a) if the Bill, having been passed by one House, has not been passed by the other House with amendments and returned to the House in which it originated, no amendment shall be proposed to the Bill other than such amendments (if any) as are made necessary by the delay in the passage of the Bill; (b) if the Bill has been so passed and returned, only such amendments as aforesaid shall be proposed to the Bill and such other amendments as are relevant to the matters with respect to which the Houses have not agreed; and the decision of the person presiding as to the amendments which are admissible under this clause shall be final. (5) A joint sitting may be held under this article and a Bill passed thereat, notwithstanding that a dissolution of the House of the People has intervened since the President notified his intention to summon the Houses to meet therein.
key_terms: amendments admissible at a joint sitting

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 108 is the constitutional deadlock-breaking mechanism for ordinary Bills (never Money Bills). If one House rejects a Bill the other passed, or the two Houses can't agree on amendments, or six months pass without action, the President may summon a joint sitting of both Houses to vote together — and since the Lok Sabha is roughly double the Rajya Sabha's size, a combined vote effectively favours the Lok Sabha's numerical strength. This mechanism has been invoked only three times in India's history (Dowry Prohibition Bill 1961, Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill 1977, POTA Bill 2002), reflecting how rare true inter-House deadlock is given the Lok Sabha's usual dominance on ordinary legislation combined with government majorities.
essential_elements: The three deadlock triggers are: outright rejection by the second House, irreconcilable disagreement on amendments, or six months' inaction by the second House
The President has discretion (not an obligation) to notify an intention to summon a joint sitting once a trigger arises
In computing the six-month period, prorogations and adjournments longer than four consecutive days are excluded, preventing artificial delay
At the joint sitting, the Bill passes by a simple majority of the combined total membership of both Houses present and voting
The presiding officer at a joint sitting is the Speaker of the House of the People (or his nominee) per Article 118(4), and his ruling on amendment admissibility is final
exceptions_and_qualifications: The joint sitting mechanism never applies to Money Bills — the proviso to clause (1) excludes them entirely, since Money Bills already have their own scheme under Article 109 where the Rajya Sabha's role is merely recommendatory
Amendments proposable at the joint sitting are tightly restricted under the proviso to clause (4) — only delay-necessitated or genuinely disputed amendments, not wholesale reopening of the Bill

Clause (5) is an express exception to Article 107(5)'s dissolution-lapsing rule — once the President has notified intention to summon a joint sitting, an intervening Lok Sabha dissolution does not kill the Bill, and the joint sitting (with the newly constituted House) may still proceed
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat clause (1)'s three sub-clauses as the trigger conditions, clause (4) as the voting mechanics (majority of the combined membership), and clause (5) as the crucial survival exception to Article 107(5) — a Bill can outlive a Lok Sabha dissolution if the President has already signalled a joint sitting.

sections.title: Special procedure in respect of Money Bills
sections.raw_text: (1) A Money Bill shall not be introduced in the Council of States. (2) After a Money Bill has been passed by the House of the People it shall be transmitted to the Council of States for its recommendations and the Council of States shall within a period of fourteen days from the date of its receipt of the Bill return the Bill to the House of the People with its recommendations and the House of the People may thereupon either accept or reject all or any of the recommendations of the Council of States. (3) If the House of the People accepts any of the recommendations of the Council of States, the Money Bill shall be deemed to have been passed by both Houses with the amendments recommended by the Council of States and accepted by the House of the People. (4) If the House of the People does not accept any of the recommendations of the Council of States, the Money Bill shall be deemed to have been passed by both Houses in the form in which it was passed by the House of the People without any of the amendments recommended by the Council of States. (5) If a Money Bill passed by the House of the People and transmitted to the Council of States for its recommendations is not returned to the House of the People within the said period of fourteen days, it shall be deemed to have been passed by both Houses at the expiration of the said period in the form in which it was passed by the House of the People.
key_terms: Money Bill introduction restricted to Lok Sabha
Lok Sabha's power to accept or reject Rajya Sabha recommendations on Money Bills
deemed passage on expiry of fourteen days

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 109 strips the Rajya Sabha of any real veto over Money Bills — it can only recommend changes within 14 days, and the Lok Sabha is free to ignore every recommendation. If the Rajya Sabha does nothing within 14 days, the Bill is deemed passed exactly as the Lok Sabha sent it. This is the sharpest asymmetry between the two Houses in the entire legislative scheme, reflecting the principle (borrowed from Westminster) that the directly elected House alone controls the public purse.
essential_elements: A Money Bill can only be introduced in the House of the People, never the Council of States
The Rajya Sabha's role is purely advisory/recommendatory — a strict 14-day window to return the Bill with recommendations
The Lok Sabha has unfettered discretion to accept or reject any or all Rajya Sabha recommendations, with no requirement to justify rejection
Silence or delay by the Rajya Sabha beyond 14 days results in automatic deemed passage in the Lok Sabha's original form
exceptions_and_qualifications: This entire special procedure is itself an exception to Article 107(1)'s general dual-origination rule and Article 107(2)'s both-Houses-must-agree rule for ordinary Bills

The joint sitting mechanism of Article 108 is expressly disapplied to Money Bills by the proviso to Article 108(1) — deadlock over a Money Bill is resolved entirely within this article's scheme, not by joint sitting

Whether a Bill actually qualifies as a 'Money Bill' at all is governed by the strict definitional test in Article 110, and that classification question is conclusively decided by the Speaker under Article 110(3) — a classification dispute (e.g., over the Aadhaar Act, 2016) can only be challenged, if at all, outside this article's own text
breakdown.how_to_read: Contrast this article's weak, time-boxed, non-binding Rajya Sabha role with the co-equal both-Houses-must-agree scheme of Article 107(2) for ordinary Bills — Money Bills are the one category where the Rajya Sabha genuinely cannot block or force amendments, only delay by a maximum of 14 days.

sections.title: Definition of "Money Bills"
sections.raw_text: (1) For the purposes of this Chapter, a Bill shall be deemed to be a Money Bill if it contains only provisions dealing with all or any of the following matters, namely:— (a) the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax; (b) the regulation of the borrowing of money or the giving of any guarantee by the Government of India, or the amendment of the law with respect to any financial obligations undertaken or to be undertaken by the Government of India; (c) the custody of the Consolidated Fund or the Contingency Fund of India, the payment of moneys into or the withdrawal of moneys from any such Fund; (d) the appropriation of moneys out of the Consolidated Fund of India; (e) the declaring of any expenditure to be expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India or the increasing of the amount of any such expenditure; (f) the receipt of money on account of the Consolidated Fund of India or the public account of India or the custody or issue of such money or the audit of the accounts of the Union or of a State; or (g) any matter incidental to any of the matters specified in sub-clauses (a) to (f). (2) A Bill shall not be deemed to be a Money Bill by reason only that it provides for the imposition of fines or other pecuniary penalties, or for the demand or payment of fees for licences or fees for services rendered, or by reason that it provides for the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax by any local authority or body for local purposes. (3) If any question arises whether a Bill is a Money Bill or not, the decision of the Speaker of the House of the People thereon shall be final. (4) There shall be endorsed on every Money Bill when it is transmitted to the Council of States under article 109, and when it is presented to the President for assent under article 111, the certificate of the Speaker of the House of the People signed by him that it is a Money Bill.
key_terms: Speaker's certification of a Money Bill
finality of Speaker's Money Bill classification

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 110 sets a deliberately narrow, exhaustive test: a Bill is a Money Bill ONLY if it deals EXCLUSIVELY with the seven listed fiscal matters (taxation, government borrowing, the Consolidated/Contingency Funds, appropriation, charged expenditure, and audit-related receipts) — plus anything merely incidental to those. If a Bill mixes a genuine fiscal provision with even one substantive non-fiscal provision, it fails the test and is an ordinary Bill (or, if fiscal-but-broader, a 'financial Bill' under Article 117 instead). Clause (3) then hands the actual classification decision — including in genuinely borderline cases — entirely to the Speaker of the Lok Sabha, whose decision is textually declared final, a provision that has generated significant controversy (e.g., over whether the Aadhaar Act, 2016 and various Finance Acts bundling unrelated amendments were correctly certified as Money Bills).
essential_elements: The Bill must contain ONLY provisions on the seven listed matters (a)-(g) — the word 'only' is the operative restrictive word making this an exhaustive, not illustrative, list
Sub-clause (g)'s 'incidental' matters must be genuinely incidental to, not independent of, the core fiscal matters

Clause (2) expressly excludes Bills merely imposing fines, penalties, licence fees, or service fees, and Bills dealing only with local-authority taxation, from Money Bill status even though they superficially touch money

The Speaker's certification under clause (4) is mandatory and must physically accompany the Bill both when sent to the Rajya Sabha under Article 109 and when presented for Presidential assent under Article 111
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (3)'s textual finality has been judicially tested — the Supreme Court in cases concerning the Aadhaar Act and later the Finance Act amendments has held that the Speaker's certification, while entitled to great weight, is not wholly beyond judicial review where a Bill is manifestly outside the Article 110(1) definition, an evolving and contested area of Money Bill jurisprudence

A Bill that is predominantly but not exclusively fiscal, and therefore fails the strict Article 110(1) test, may instead qualify as a 'financial Bill' under Article 117, which follows a different (less Rajya-Sabha-restrictive) procedure
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat clause (1)'s seven sub-clauses as a closed list and the word 'only' as the exhaustivity trigger; treat clause (3) as vesting the classification decision in the Speaker while flagging that this finality has been contested in modern litigation over bundled Finance Acts.

sections.title: Assent to Bills
sections.raw_text: When a Bill has been passed by the Houses of Parliament, it shall be presented to the President, and the President shall declare either that he assents to the Bill, or that he withholds assent therefrom: Provided that the President may, as soon as possible after the presentation to him of a Bill for assent, return the Bill if it is not a Money Bill to the Houses with a message requesting that they will reconsider the Bill or any specified provisions thereof and, in particular, will consider the desirability of introducing any such amendments as he may recommend in his message, and when a Bill is so returned, the Houses shall reconsider the Bill accordingly, and if the Bill is passed again by the Houses with or without amendment and presented to the President for assent, the President shall not withhold assent therefrom.
key_terms: President's power to return a Bill for reconsideration

breakdown.plain_summary: Once both Houses have passed a Bill, it goes to the President for assent — the final step before it becomes law. Article 111 gives the President three theoretical options: assent, withhold assent, or (for any Bill except a Money Bill) send it back once with a message asking Parliament to reconsider it or specific provisions. But the proviso's final clause closes the loop: if Parliament passes the Bill again, with or without the President's suggested amendments, the President has no further choice — assent becomes mandatory. This effectively makes the 'return' power a delaying/suasive tool rather than a true veto, and in practice modern Presidents have sometimes left Bills pending indefinitely (a so-called 'pocket veto') rather than formally withholding assent, since the Article's text sets no deadline for the President's initial decision.
essential_elements: Ordinary Bills passed by both Houses (or at a joint sitting) must be presented to the President for assent, withholding, or (once) return for reconsideration
The return-for-reconsideration option is unavailable for Money Bills — the proviso's 'if it is not a Money Bill' carve-out means Money Bills can only be assented to or withheld, never sent back
Reconsideration by Parliament following a return may or may not adopt the President's recommended amendments — the Houses are free to re-pass the Bill in its original form
Once re-passed after reconsideration, Presidential assent becomes obligatory — 'the President shall not withhold assent therefrom'
exceptions_and_qualifications: No express time limit is fixed within which the President must act on a Bill (in contrast to the equivalent State-level provision, Article 200, which does not itself fix a timeline either but has become the subject of a Supreme Court-imposed deadline in later jurisprudence) — this silence is the textual root of the 'pocket veto' practice and associated constitutional debate
The proviso's protection is a one-time-only mechanism — there is no repeated cycle of return; a single re-passage after reconsideration exhausts the President's discretion entirely
breakdown.how_to_read: Read the main clause as the basic assent/withhold binary, and the proviso as a qualified 'suspensive veto' available only once and only for non-Money Bills — the absence of any textual deadline is the key practitioner point behind the modern 'pocket veto' controversy.

sections.title: Annual financial statement
sections.raw_text: (1) The President shall in respect of every financial year cause to be laid before both the Houses of Parliament a statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government of India for that year, in this Part referred to as the "annual financial statement''. (2) The estimates of expenditure embodied in the annual financial statement shall show separately— (a) the sums required to meet expenditure described by this Constitution as expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India; and (b) the sums required to meet other expenditure proposed to be made from the Consolidated Fund of India, and shall distinguish expenditure on revenue account from other expenditure. (3) The following expenditure shall be expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India— (a) the emoluments and allowances of the President and other expenditure relating to his office; (b) the salaries and allowances of the Chairman and the Deputy Chairman of the Council of States and the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the House of the People; (c) debt charges for which the Government of India is liable including interest, sinking fund charges and redemption charges, and other expenditure relating to the raising of loans and the service and redemption of debt; (d) (i) the salaries, allowances and pensions payable to or in respect of Judges of the Supreme Court; (ii) the pensions payable to or in respect of Judges of the Federal Court; (iii) the pensions payable to or in respect of Judges of any High Court which exercises jurisdiction in relation to any area included in the territory of India or which at any time before the commencement of this Constitution exercised jurisdiction in relation to any area included in a Governor's Province of the Dominion of India; (e) the salary, allowances and pension payable to or in respect of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India; (f) any sums required to satisfy any judgment, decree or award of any court or arbitral tribunal; (g) any other expenditure declared by this Constitution or by Parliament by law to be so charged.
key_terms: expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the constitutional basis for what is popularly called the 'Union Budget' — the President (in practice, on the Finance Minister's presentation) must place before Parliament every year a statement of expected income and spending. Clause (2) requires the estimate to split 'charged' expenditure (listed in clause (3)) from ordinary 'voted' expenditure, because — as Article 113 makes clear — only the voted portion is actually put to a Parliamentary vote; the charged portion (high constitutional offices' salaries, debt-servicing, court judgments) is insulated from being voted down, protecting institutional independence and India's credit obligations from ordinary political majorities.
essential_elements: The President must cause an annual financial statement to be laid before both Houses for every financial year
The statement must separately show charged expenditure (clause 3's closed list) versus other proposed expenditure, and must distinguish revenue-account from other expenditure

The charged-expenditure list (clause 3) includes the President's and Vice-President-adjacent presiding officers' emoluments, all public debt servicing, Supreme Court and (historically) Federal Court and certain High Court judges' salaries/pensions, the CAG's salary and pension, and court/arbitral-award satisfaction sums
Clause (3)(g) is an open-ended residual category allowing the Constitution itself or Parliament by ordinary law to add further charged items
exceptions_and_qualifications: Charged expenditure is deliberately insulated from the ordinary voting process under Article 113(1) — Parliament may discuss it but cannot vote it down, distinguishing it sharply from the 'demands for grants' regime for other expenditure under Article 113(2)

The reference to Federal Court pensions and pre-Constitution High Court judges is a historical relic addressing transitional judicial personnel from British India and princely-state successor courts, of limited contemporary operative significance but still technically in force
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat clause (3)'s seven sub-clauses as the fixed 'charged' list that Article 113 later exempts from voting — this article is best read together with Article 113 as a single charged-vs-voted budgetary scheme.

sections.title: Procedure in Parliament with respect to estimates
sections.raw_text: (1) So much of the estimates as relates to expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India shall not be submitted to the vote of Parliament, but nothing in this clause shall be construed as preventing the discussion in either House of Parliament of any of those estimates. (2) So much of the said estimates as relates to other expenditure shall be submitted in the form of demands for grants to the House of the People, and the House of the People shall have power to assent, or to refuse to assent, to any demand, or to assent to any demand subject to a reduction of the amount specified therein. (3) No demand for a grant shall be made except on the recommendation of the President.
key_terms: exemption of charged expenditure from voting
House of the People's power to reduce or refuse a grant
Presidential recommendation precondition for grant demands

breakdown.plain_summary: This article operationalises the charged/voted split from Article 112. Charged expenditure is immune from an up-or-down vote (though Parliament can still debate it) — protecting things like judicial salaries and debt payments from being weaponised in ordinary politics. Everything else must be formally proposed to the Lok Sabha alone as individual 'demands for grants' (department by department), and the Lok Sabha can accept, reject, or cut down (but never increase) each demand — the 'cut motion' practice familiar from Indian Budget sessions flows directly from this clause. Clause (3) adds a gatekeeping rule: no spending demand can even be tabled without the President's prior recommendation, reinforcing executive control over the public purse's initiation (mirroring the President's-recommendation requirement for Money Bills under Article 117).
essential_elements: Charged expenditure estimates are excluded from any Parliamentary vote, but discussion of them in either House remains fully permitted
Non-charged ('voted') expenditure must be presented as itemised demands for grants exclusively to the House of the People (not the Council of States)
The Lok Sabha's power over a demand is one-directional — it may assent in full, refuse entirely, or reduce the amount, but it has no power to increase any demand
Every demand for a grant requires the President's prior recommendation before it can even be moved
exceptions_and_qualifications: The exclusivity of the Lok Sabha's grant-voting role parallels, but is textually distinct from, the Rajya Sabha's total exclusion from Money Bill introduction under Article 109(1) — here the Rajya Sabha has no role at all, not even a recommendatory one

The 'cannot be increased' limitation on the Lok Sabha's grant power is a strict ceiling flowing from the executive's exclusive power to propose (and thereby cap) spending, reflected again in clause (3)'s recommendation requirement
breakdown.how_to_read: Pair clause (1)'s vote exemption with Article 112(3)'s charged list, and read clause (2)'s 'assent, refuse, or reduce (never increase)' formula as the textual source of the Budget session's 'cut motion' procedure that Indian practitioners will recognise from parliamentary practice.

sections.title: Appropriation Bills
sections.raw_text: (1) As soon as may be after the grants under article 113 have been made by the House of the People, there shall be introduced a Bill to provide for the appropriation out of the Consolidated Fund of India of all moneys required to meet— (a) the grants so made by the House of the People; and (b) the expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India but not exceeding in any case the amount shown in the statement previously laid before Parliament. (2) No amendment shall be proposed to any such Bill in either House of Parliament which will have the effect of varying the amount or altering the destination of any grant so made or of varying the amount of any expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, and the decision of the person presiding as to whether an amendment is inadmissible under this clause shall be final. (3) Subject to the provisions of articles 115 and 116, no money shall be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India except under appropriation made by law passed in accordance with the provisions of this article.
key_terms: bar on amendments varying grants or charged expenditure
no withdrawal from Consolidated Fund without appropriation law

breakdown.plain_summary: After the Lok Sabha votes on demands for grants under Article 113, that approval alone doesn't yet authorise any actual spending — a formal Appropriation Bill must be passed converting the voted grants (plus the pre-fixed charged expenditure) into binding legal authority to draw money from the Consolidated Fund. Clause (2) locks the Bill down tightly: no amendment in either House can change the amount or purpose of any grant, or alter charged expenditure figures, because those figures were already fixed by the earlier grant-voting and budget-statement process — this Bill is purely a formalisation, not a fresh policy debate. Clause (3) then states the constitutional bedrock rule: government cannot spend a rupee from the Consolidated Fund without this Bill (or the interim mechanisms of Articles 115-116).
essential_elements: An Appropriation Bill must be introduced promptly after grants are made under Article 113, covering both the voted grants and the charged expenditure up to the previously stated amounts
Amendments that would vary a grant's amount or destination, or alter charged expenditure figures, are constitutionally inadmissible in either House
The presiding officer's ruling on whether a proposed amendment is inadmissible under clause (2) is final and not open to further challenge within the House
No money may leave the Consolidated Fund of India except under an appropriation made via this article's Bill process (or the Article 115/116 exceptions)
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (3)'s absolute bar is expressly made subject to Articles 115 (supplementary/additional/excess grants) and 116 (votes on account, votes of credit, exceptional grants) — those provide the exceptional/interim funding mechanisms bridging gaps this article's ordinary annual process does not cover

The amendment bar in clause (2) does not prevent debate or discussion on the Bill generally — it specifically targets amendments that would alter already-fixed grant amounts, destinations, or charged expenditure figures
breakdown.how_to_read: Read this article as the final formal-legalisation step following the Article 112 statement and Article 113 grant-voting — clause (3) is the 'no money without an Appropriation Act' rule that every Indian budget cycle ultimately rests on, subject only to the Article 115/116 bridge mechanisms.
